# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

---

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and a speaker label — that is what the
SQLite rows and the JSONL lines carry. Saved clips (`save_clips`, on by default
in the Python core) are the one place raw audio lands, and it lands on local
disk under the single home directory, never anywhere else. New persisted fields
follow the same split; if a feature wants audio, it belongs in `clips/`, under
the user's existing choice, not in a new location.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.** `~/.laughcounter` for the Python
core (overridable via `LAUGHCOUNTER_HOME`), `~/Library/Application
Support/LaughCounter/` for the app. "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a
documented property — don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it.

**The one accepted egress is a model download in an optional extra.** The
`[yamnet]` extra fetches the TF-Hub handle in `detector/yamnet.py`, and the
`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.

**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
It binds loopback by default; `--host 0.0.0.0` is the user reaching it from their
phone, and the mutating endpoints require an `application/json` content type so a
browser must preflight cross-origin (`dashboard.py`'s `do_POST`). Any new
mutating endpoint keeps that guard; nothing else stands between the LAN and the
laugh log.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

8	the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
9	device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
10	Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
11	*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
12	overlap restarts. (#22)

14	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself
15	
16	`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
17	`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
18	a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
19	terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
20	those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
21	SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal
22	default. SIGKILL/Force-Quit/crash remain uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug.
23	Don't add `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` to Info.plist: it would let logout
24	SIGKILL the app past all of this.
25	
26	## Deferred work must be generation-guarded
27	
28	`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
29	delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
30	stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or
31	un-settled at wake. Every intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every
32	delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.
33	When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /
34	`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
35	all future starts.
36	
37	## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop
38

40	(react → infinite restart loop, hence the suppress window) **and** for genuine
41	device events — including while the machine heads into sleep (hence the
42	`sleeping` gate from `willSleep` until the post-wake settle). A genuine event
43	swallowed by the window is reconciled at settle time by *state*, not by the
44	notification: engine dead while `listening` → restart; start failed and an
45	event arrived → one retry per swallowed event (a dead mic emits no events, so

# macOS audio lifecycle — releasing the mic on every path

Hard-won rules for `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` (AudioHub, AppDelegate's restart
machinery, VoiceCommand). Read before touching engine start/stop, sleep/wake, or
exit handling.

**The invariant.** If this process ends — or intentionally stops capture — while
the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
overlap restarts. (#22)

## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself

`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal
default. SIGKILL/Force-Quit/crash remain uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug.
Don't add `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` to Info.plist: it would let logout
SIGKILL the app past all of this.

## Deferred work must be generation-guarded

`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or
un-settled at wake. Every intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every
delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.
When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /
`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
all future starts.

## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop

CoreAudio posts `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` for our *own* stop/start
(react → infinite restart loop, hence the suppress window) **and** for genuine
device events — including while the machine heads into sleep (hence the
`sleeping` gate from `willSleep` until the post-wake settle). A genuine event
swallowed by the window is reconciled at settle time by *state*, not by the
notification: engine dead while `listening` → restart; start failed and an
event arrived → one retry per swallowed event (a dead mic emits no events, so
this can't poll).

## Misc gotchas that bit

- `engine.stop()` unconditionally in `AudioHub.stop()`: it's safe when not
  running and it releases what `prepare()` allocated — a prepare-then-throw
  path would otherwise keep the input unit holding the device.
- `installTap` with a format the hardware no longer matches raises an
  **uncatchable NSException** — re-validate the live format immediately before
  the tap (narrows, doesn't eliminate; there is no atomic API).
- `SFSpeechRecognizer` fed via `SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest` never
  holds the device — it can't cause the wedge. But its state is touched from
  main, the Speech callback queue, *and* the audio tap thread: everything in
  `VoiceCommand` goes through one lock, and the two-phase `start()` gates the
  task store on *request identity* (`request === newRequest`), because a
  restart() between the phases leaves `running == true` — gating on `running`
  would store a dead task and permanently block the idempotency guard.

# LaughCounter — local project procedures

Project-specific instructions for this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
canon (vendored into the repo, read-only). Where a local rule refines a canon
rule, the local one wins — it carries this project's concrete files and gotchas.
Routing index, not a payload: read the matching doc when its trigger fires; don't
pre-load.

Capture lessons **here, locally**, in the doc that owns the topic. A lesson's
*portability* is Claudinite's concern (its growth routine lifts portable lessons
up into the shared canon) — not a reason to capture it anywhere else.

- [ci-release.md](ci-release.md) — **before touching the release/CI workflows
  (`.github/workflows/*-macos-dmg.yml`).** How the DMG gets published to GitHub
  Releases, and the trigger gotchas learned wiring it up.
- [mac-audio-lifecycle.md](mac-audio-lifecycle.md) — **before touching engine
  start/stop, sleep/wake, exit handling, or `VoiceCommand` in
  `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/`.** The release-the-mic-on-every-path invariant
  (USB webcam mics wedge otherwise), signal routing, generation-guarded deferred
  work, and config-change reconciliation.

@ci-release.md

# CI & release — the macOS DMG

How `LaughCounter.dmg` reaches users, and the workflow-trigger gotchas learned
wiring it up. Read before editing `.github/workflows/release-macos-dmg.yml` or
`build-macos-dmg.yml`.

**The shape.** `release-macos-dmg.yml` owns `main`: on a push to `main` touching
`mac/**` it builds the DMG, derives `v<version>` from `mac/Resources/Info.plist`,
and creates/updates that GitHub Release with `LaughCounter.dmg` attached — so the
README's stable `releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg` link always resolves.
`build-macos-dmg.yml` is the feature-branch artifact builder and **excludes
`main`** (`branches: ["**", "!main"]`) so it never duplicates the release build.

## Trigger the release on push-to-main, not a `v*` tag push

A Claude Code **web session pushes through a git-only proxy that cannot push
`v*` tags**, so a release workflow keyed on `push: tags` never fires from a
session — the Release area stays empty and the `latest/download` link 404s. Key
the release on **push to `main`** (scoped to `mac/**`) instead: the job derives
`v<version>` from `Info.plist` and creates the tag + Release with `GITHUB_TOKEN`,
which *can* tag and release from within Actions even though the session can't.
(#18 / #19)

## A UI-published Release does not fire `push: tags` — add `release: published`

Publishing a Release from the GitHub UI creates the tag but does **not** emit a
`push: tags` event, so a workflow listening only for tag pushes won't build for
it. Keep a `release: types: [published]` trigger alongside the push-to-main one so
a hand-published Release still builds and attaches the DMG. (#11 / #13)

## Why the two triggers don't loop or double-build

- The tag + Release the push-to-main job creates is made with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and
  a Release created by `GITHUB_TOKEN` does **not** re-fire the `release` event —
  so the `release: published` trigger doesn't re-run it. (This is the canon's
  general "`GITHUB_TOKEN` doesn't start another workflow" rule, applied to the
  `release` event specifically.)
- `build-macos-dmg.yml` excludes `main`, so a `mac/**` push to `main` builds once
  (in the release job), not twice.

## Signing & notarization is an optional, secret-gated lane (#4)

Both DMG workflows have an **optional** Developer ID signing + Apple notarization
lane that runs only when the signing secrets are set (`MACOS_CERT_P12`,
`MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD`, `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`,
`APPLE_APP_PASSWORD`); without them the build still passes and ships an **ad-hoc**
DMG. **Keep it secret-gated** — never make signing a required step, or a fork or
secret-less build breaks. The signing/notarization how-to and the user-facing
Gatekeeper steps live in `mac/README.md`; `scripts/build-app.sh` signs and
`scripts/notarize-dmg.sh` notarizes + staples. The CI-side gotchas that aren't in
the README:

- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`),
  and under it the mic needs an explicit entitlement
  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, in
  `mac/Resources/LaughCounter.entitlements`) that an ad-hoc build doesn't — so
  turning on notarization silently kills mic access unless the entitlement ships
  with it. (Speech recognition is gated by TCC + the Info.plist usage string, not
  a codesign entitlement, so it needs nothing there.)
- **An ad-hoc signature can't be notarized** — they're separate lanes; only the
  Developer-ID-signed `.app` (built when `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY` is set) can be
  submitted to the notary service.
- **The ephemeral signing keychain must be added to the searchable keychain
  list** (`security list-keychains -d user -s "$KEYCHAIN" $(security
  list-keychains -d user | sed …)`) or `codesign` can't find the imported
  identity. That `sed` pipe is why the workflows set `defaults.run.shell: bash`
  for pipefail (#27; enforced by the canon `gha/run-pipefail` check).
- **macOS 15 (Sequoia) removed the right-click → Open Gatekeeper bypass** — the
  ad-hoc install path is now System Settings → Privacy & Security → *Open Anyway*,
  or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>` (see `mac/README.md`).
- This is the **non–App Store** track (no App Sandbox); a Mac App Store build
  would need the App Sandbox and a different Apple Distribution certificate.

2	import AVFoundation
3	import Speech

5	final class AppDelegate: NSObject, NSApplicationDelegate {
6	    private var statusItem: NSStatusItem!
7	    private let store = LaughStore()
8	    private let counter = LaughCounter()
9	    private let audio = AudioHub()
10	    private let detector = LaughDetector()
11	    private let voice = VoiceCommand()
12	    private var micGranted = false
13	    private var listening = false
14	    // (Re)starting the engine itself posts .AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange, so
15	    // we suppress that notification around our own (re)starts to avoid a restart
16	    // loop that would keep the engine from ever running long enough to detect.
17	    private var suppressConfigChange = false
18	    // Single-flight + rate-limit for (re)starts: repeatedly stop/starting a USB
19	    // mic in quick succession can wedge it, so restarts can never overlap or
20	    // rapid-cycle — an extra request while one is in flight is coalesced to one.
21	    private var restartInFlight = false
22	    private var restartQueued = false
23	    // Every intentional stop (sleep, terminate) and every accepted restart bumps
24	    // this; the delayed finishListening/settle closures capture it when scheduled
25	    // and abort if it moved. Without it, a stop can't cancel the +0.4s restart it
26	    // raced with — sleep during that gap would start the engine going *into*
27	    // sleep (carrying a live IOProc into sleep, the wedge condition), or fire it
28	    // at wake before the hardware settles. asyncAfter timers scheduled before
29	    // sleep fire immediately ON wake, which makes this race very reachable.
30	    private var restartGeneration = 0
31	    // A config-change notification arrived while suppressConfigChange was up.
32	    // The suppression must swallow our own stop/start echoes (reacting to them
33	    // would loop), but it can also swallow a *genuine* device event — noted here
34	    // so the settle closure can reconcile by state instead of losing the event.
35	    private var configChangeSwallowed = false
36	    // True from willSleep until the post-wake settle delay ends. Gates both
37	    // requestListening and the config-change handler: CoreAudio tears down /
38	    // switches devices while the machine heads into sleep, and reacting to those
39	    // notifications would restart capture into sleep right after the intentional
40	    // willSleep teardown.
41	    private var sleeping = false
42	    // Speech may only auto-(re)start once authorization was actually granted.
43	    private var speechAuthorized = false
44	
45	    // Opt-in "keep the Mac awake so it keeps hearing laughs during a long movie".
46	    // Off by default; the choice persists across launches. While enabled *and*
47	    // listening we hold a power assertion that blocks idle *system* sleep (the
48	    // display can still sleep — we only need audio to keep running). It does not
49	    // block lid-close or a manual Sleep, and it costs battery, so it's opt-in.
50	    private let keepAwakeDefaultsKey = "keepMacAwakeWhileListening"
51	    private var keepAwake = false
52	    private var sleepAssertion: NSObjectProtocol?
53	
54	    func applicationDidFinishLaunching(_ notification: Notification) {
55	        statusItem = NSStatusBar.system.statusItem(withLength: NSStatusItem.variableLength)
56	        keepAwake = UserDefaults.standard.bool(forKey: keepAwakeDefaultsKey)  // false if unset
57	        refreshTitle()
58	        buildMenu()
59	        wireUp()
60	        observeSystemEvents()
61	        AppLog.shared.log("app launched")
62	        requestPermissionsAndStart()
63	    }
64	
65	    // MARK: wiring
66	
67	    private func wireUp() {
68	        // A counted laugh → log it with the you-vs-TV hypothesis, and blip only for
69	        // *your* laughs (blipping at every TV laugh would be maddening).
70	        counter.onLaugh = { [weak self] event in
71	            guard let self = self else { return }
72	            self.store.append(event)
73	            AppLog.shared.log(String(format: "laugh logged origin=%@ peak=%.2f dur=%.2f — %@",
74	                                     event.origin, event.peak, event.duration, event.originReason))
75	            if event.origin == "me" { Chime.play(times: 1) }
76	            DispatchQueue.main.async { self.refreshTitle() }
77	        }
78	        // Sub-threshold episode → log it as a candidate (silent, uncounted) so later
79	        // "I laughed" feedback has a nearby event to align to.
80	        counter.onCandidate = { [weak self] event in
81	            self?.store.append(event, label: "candidate")
82	            AppLog.shared.log(String(format: "candidate logged origin=%@ peak=%.2f dur=%.2f — %@",
83	                                     event.origin, event.peak, event.duration, event.originReason))
84	        }
85	        // Each analysis window → feed the counter (real audio timing inside).
86	        detector.onObservation = { [weak self] obs in
87	            self?.counter.update(obs)
88	        }
89	        // "I just laughed": spoken command vs the menu/keyboard get different sources.
90	        voice.onTrigger = { [weak self] in self?.markMissed(source: "voice") }
91	        // One mic tap, fanned out to both consumers.
92	        audio.onBuffer = { [weak self] buffer, when in
93	            self?.detector.analyze(buffer, at: when)
94	            self?.voice.append(buffer)
95	        }
96	    }
97	
98	    private func markMissed(source: String) {
99	        store.appendMissed(source: source)
100	        AppLog.shared.log("missed laugh logged via \(source)")
101	        Chime.play(times: 2)
102	        DispatchQueue.main.async { self.refreshTitle() }
103	    }
104	
105	    // MARK: permissions + start
106	
107	    private func requestPermissionsAndStart() {
108	        AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .audio) { [weak self] granted in
109	            DispatchQueue.main.async {
110	                guard let self = self else { return }
111	                self.micGranted = granted
112	                if granted {
113	                    self.requestListening()
114	                    self.requestSpeech()
115	                } else {
116	                    AppLog.shared.log("microphone access denied", level: "ERROR")
117	                    self.showMicDenied()
118	                }
119	            }
120	        }
121	    }
122	
123	    /// Single-flight, rate-limited entry to (re)start listening. Every trigger
124	    /// (launch, wake, config-change, manual resume) goes through here so the audio
125	    /// engine can never overlap-restart or rapid-cycle — which can wedge a USB mic.
126	    /// Tears down, lets the input device settle briefly, then re-acquires.
127	    private func requestListening() {
128	        guard micGranted else { return }
129	        if sleeping {                  // heading into (or settling out of) sleep:
130	            // the post-wake resume is the one path out; log so a swallowed manual
131	            // click is visible in the activity log rather than silently ignored
132	            AppLog.shared.log("listening request ignored (sleep transition in progress)")
133	            return
134	        }
135	        if restartInFlight {           // coalesce; don't stack restarts
136	            restartQueued = true
137	            return
138	        }
139	        restartInFlight = true
140	        suppressConfigChange = true    // ignore the config-changes our stop/start emits
141	        configChangeSwallowed = false  // fresh window; note only events from this cycle
142	        restartGeneration &+= 1
143	        let generation = restartGeneration
144	        counter.flush()
145	        counter.reset()
146	        detector.reset()
147	        audio.stop()
148	        listening = false
149	        refreshTitle()
150	        // Let the (USB) input device release before re-acquiring — reacquiring
151	        // immediately after teardown is what can wedge some USB mics.
152	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 0.4) { [weak self] in
153	            self?.finishListening(generation: generation)
154	        }
155	    }
156	
157	    private func finishListening(generation: Int) {
158	        // A stop (sleep/terminate) superseded this restart while it waited — the
159	        // mic must stay released, not be re-acquired behind the stop's back.
160	        guard generation == restartGeneration else { return }
161	        do {
162	            // Configure the analyzer BEFORE audio flows, so no early buffers are
163	            // dropped and analysis reliably starts (matches the original order).
164	            let format = try audio.prepareFormat()
165	            try detector.configure(format: format)
166	            try audio.start(format: format)
167	            listening = true
168	            AppLog.shared.log("listening started "
169	                + "(sampleRate=\(Int(format.sampleRate)), channels=\(format.channelCount))")
170	        } catch {
171	            audio.stop()
172	            listening = false
173	            AppLog.shared.log("could not start listening: \(error.localizedDescription)",
174	                              level: "ERROR")
175	        }
176	        refreshTitle()
177	        buildMenu()
178	        // Settle window: no further restart (or config-change reaction) until the
179	        // engine has run undisturbed for a moment. Then honor any coalesced request.
180	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 1.2) { [weak self] in
181	            guard let self = self, generation == self.restartGeneration else { return }
182	            self.suppressConfigChange = false
183	            self.restartInFlight = false
184	            let swallowed = self.configChangeSwallowed
185	            self.configChangeSwallowed = false
186	            if self.restartQueued {
187	                self.restartQueued = false
188	                self.requestListening()
189	            } else if self.listening && !self.audio.isRunning {
190	                // A genuine config change landed inside the suppress window and
191	                // halted the engine (AVAudioEngine stops rendering when the
192	                // device changes under it). The suppression rightly ignored the
193	                // notification — self-emitted ones would loop — so reconcile by
194	                // state instead: "listening" but engine dead means we owe a
195	                // restart, otherwise the UI claims listening while nothing flows.
196	                AppLog.shared.log("engine halted during settle — restarting", level: "WARN")
197	                self.requestListening()
198	            } else if !self.listening && swallowed {
199	                // Complementary case: this cycle's start FAILED (no device yet),
200	                // and the device's arrival notification landed inside the window.
201	                // Dropping it would leave the app "not listening" with no further
202	                // event to recover on. One retry per swallowed event — a dead mic
203	                // emits no events, so this can't poll forever.
204	                AppLog.shared.log("device event during settle after failed start — retrying")
205	                self.requestListening()
206	            }
207	        }
208	    }

210	    private func stopListening(reason: String) {
211	        // Invalidate the whole in-flight restart machinery, not just the queue
212	        // flag: a pending finishListening must never fire after an intentional
213	        // stop (it would re-acquire the mic right as the system sleeps), and the
214	        // in-flight/suppress latches must not stay stuck blocking future starts.
215	        restartGeneration &+= 1
216	        restartInFlight = false
217	        restartQueued = false
218	        suppressConfigChange = false
219	        counter.flush()
220	        voice.stop()     // symmetric with resume; recognition restarts on wake
221	        audio.stop()
222	        listening = false
223	        AppLog.shared.log("listening stopped (\(reason))")
224	        refreshTitle()
225	        buildMenu()
226	    }

263	    @objc private func didWake() {
264	        AppLog.shared.log("system woke — resuming listening shortly")
265	        // Stay gated (`sleeping`) through the settle delay so wake-time device
266	        // re-enumeration can't trigger an early, un-settled restart; the resume

271	        let generation = restartGeneration

274	            self.sleeping = false
275	            self.requestListening()
276	            if self.speechAuthorized { self.voice.start() }   // idempotent
277	        }
278	    }

386	    /// Clean up before the process exits. Reached for every exit path that goes
387	    /// through `NSApp.terminate` — the menu Quit item, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown
388	    /// quit Apple Event, and the SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP sources in main.swift that
389	    /// route catchable signals here. Not reached for SIGKILL (Force Quit,
390	    /// `kill -9`) or a crash — those are uncatchable; nothing in-process can
391	    /// release the mic on them.
392	    ///
393	    /// Releasing the microphone here is the whole point: if the process dies with
394	    /// the input tap still installed and the engine running, its CoreAudio IOProc
395	    /// stays registered on the input device. Some USB webcam mics get wedged by
396	    /// that and go silent — no input registered in System Settings — until they're
397	    /// physically unplugged and reconnected. Tearing down the tap + engine (and the
398	    /// speech recogniser, which also holds the audio stream) deregisters the IOProc
399	    /// so the device is handed cleanly back to the system.
400	    func applicationWillTerminate(_ notification: Notification) {
401	        sleeping = true          // gate any late config-change reaction during teardown
402	        // stopListening: flushes the in-progress laugh, invalidates pending
403	        // restarts (generation bump), stops speech, removes the tap, stops the
404	        // engine, and (via refreshTitle) drops the keep-awake assertion.
405	        stopListening(reason: "app terminating")

3	/// A competing (non-laugh) sound class and its confidence, kept for TV
4	/// de-confliction and false-positive debugging.
5	struct ContextScore {
6	    let label: String
7	    let confidence: Double
8	}
9	
10	/// One episode of detected laughter (not a single frame — a whole laugh).
11	struct LaughEvent {
12	    let start: Double   // epoch seconds
13	    let end: Double
14	    let duration: Double
15	    let peak: Double
16	    let mean: Double
17	    let type: String            // which laugh class dominated ("" if unknown)
18	    let context: [ContextScore] // top non-laugh classes heard during the episode
19	    let origin: String          // hypothesis about the source: "me" | "tv"
20	    let originReason: String    // human-readable why, for the activity log
21	    let tvSignal: Double        // strongest produced-audio context confidence (0…1)
22	}
23	
24	/// One analysed window handed to the counter. Carries the *real* audio timing
25	/// (from `SNClassificationResult.timeRange`) plus the winning laugh class and the
26	/// strongest TV-context class, so durations are accurate and TV audio can be told
27	/// apart from a person laughing in the room.
28	struct LaughObservation {
29	    let time: Double            // epoch seconds of the window start (real audio time)
30	    let windowDuration: Double  // real window length from SoundAnalysis
31	    let laughScore: Double      // max confidence across laugh classes
32	    let laughType: String       // which laugh class won ("" if none)
33	    let contextScore: Double    // max confidence across TV-context classes
34	    let contextLabel: String    // which TV-context class was strongest
35	    let context: [ContextScore] // a few top non-laugh classes (for logging)
36	}
37	
38	/// Turns a stream of per-window observations into discrete laughs, using a
39	/// hysteresis state machine:
40	///
41	/// * start tracking when confidence rises to `enterThreshold`,
42	/// * keep going while it stays above the lower `exitThreshold` (hysteresis),
43	/// * bridge silences shorter than `mergeGap` (a fit of giggles = one laugh),
44	/// * only record episodes lasting at least `minDuration`.
45	///
46	/// An episode is **counted** as a real laugh only if its peak confidence reaches
47	/// `countThreshold`. Episodes that clear the lower `enterThreshold` but not
48	/// `countThreshold` are emitted as **candidates** (`onCandidate`) — logged for
49	/// later analysis / threshold tuning, but not counted.
50	///
51	/// Episode length comes from the observations' real window bounds, so a laugh
52	/// that spans several windows reports its true duration instead of a fixed 0.5s.
53	/// Deterministic and I/O-free.
54	final class LaughCounter {
55	    /// Peak confidence an episode must reach to be *counted* as a real laugh.
56	    var countThreshold = 0.5
57	    /// Lower bar at which we start tracking an episode at all. Deliberately low so
58	    /// near-misses are logged as candidates too — later "I laughed" feedback can be
59	    /// aligned against a nearby low-confidence event instead of nothing.
60	    var enterThreshold = 0.15
61	    /// Hysteresis exit — an open episode stays open while confidence holds above this.
62	    var exitThreshold = 0.1
63	    var minDuration = 0.4
64	    // Bridge gaps up to this long so one laugh spanning several analysis windows
65	    // is one episode, not several. The built-in classifier emits ~3s windows
66	    // every ~1.5s, so this must exceed that hop or every overlapping window
67	    // becomes its own (duplicate) laugh with a fixed ~3s duration.
68	    var mergeGap = 2.0
69	    var frameSeconds = 0.5   // fallback window length if the API doesn't supply one
70	
71	    /// Emit sub-threshold episodes (peak below `countThreshold`) via `onCandidate`.
72	    var logCandidates = true
73	
74	    /// You-vs-TV attribution: if the strongest "produced-audio" context class
75	    /// (music / speech / audience / instruments) reaches this confidence, the
76	    /// episode is hypothesised to come from the TV rather than a person in the
77	    /// room. A guess, not a verdict — laughs are still logged, just attributed.
78	    var tvThreshold = 0.3
79	
80	    /// Called (on the caller's thread) when a counted laugh is finalised. The
81	    /// event's `origin` carries the you-vs-TV hypothesis.
82	    var onLaugh: ((LaughEvent) -> Void)?
83	    /// Called for a sub-threshold episode (peak < `countThreshold`) — logged for
84	    /// alignment/tuning, not counted. Also carries an `origin` hypothesis.
85	    var onCandidate: ((LaughEvent) -> Void)?
86	
87	    private var start: Double?
88	    private var lastActive = 0.0
89	    private var lastWindow = 0.5
90	    private var peak = 0.0
91	    private var sum = 0.0
92	    private var n = 0
93	    private var peakType = ""
94	    private var peakContext = 0.0
95	    private var peakContextLabel = ""
96	    private var contextAgg: [String: Double] = [:]
97	    private var lastTs: Double?
98	
99	    func update(_ obs: LaughObservation) {
100	        if let last = lastTs, obs.time < last { return }  // ignore backward time
101	        lastTs = obs.time
102	
103	        let loud = obs.laughScore >= enterThreshold
104	        let soft = obs.laughScore >= exitThreshold
105	
106	        // Close a stale episode first, regardless of this window's loudness, so a
107	        // laugh resuming after a > mergeGap silence is a new laugh, not a merge.
108	        if start != nil && obs.time - lastActive > mergeGap {
109	            finalizeEpisode()
110	        }
111	
112	        if start == nil {
113	            if loud { begin(obs) }
114	        } else if soft {
115	            extend(obs)
116	        }
117	    }
118	
119	    /// Finalise any episode still open (e.g. on shutdown or before a pause).
120	    func flush() {
121	        if start != nil { finalizeEpisode() }
122	    }
123	
124	    /// Drop all state, including the stream clock — call when (re)starting the
125	    /// audio stream so the new stream's timestamps aren't rejected as "backward".
126	    func reset() {
127	        resetEpisode()
128	        lastTs = nil
129	    }
130	
131	    private func begin(_ o: LaughObservation) {
132	        start = o.time; lastActive = o.time; lastWindow = o.windowDuration
133	        peak = o.laughScore; sum = o.laughScore; n = 1; peakType = o.laughType
134	        peakContext = o.contextScore; peakContextLabel = o.contextLabel
135	        contextAgg = [:]; accumulateContext(o)
136	    }
137	
138	    private func extend(_ o: LaughObservation) {
139	        lastActive = o.time; lastWindow = o.windowDuration
140	        if o.laughScore > peak { peak = o.laughScore; peakType = o.laughType }
141	        sum += o.laughScore; n += 1
142	        if o.contextScore > peakContext { peakContext = o.contextScore; peakContextLabel = o.contextLabel }
143	        accumulateContext(o)
144	    }
145	
146	    private func accumulateContext(_ o: LaughObservation) {
147	        for c in o.context {
148	            contextAgg[c.label] = max(contextAgg[c.label] ?? 0, c.confidence)
149	        }
150	    }
151	
152	    private func finalizeEpisode() {
153	        guard let s = start else { return }
154	        let end = lastActive + (lastWindow > 0 ? lastWindow : frameSeconds)
155	        let duration = end - s
156	        let capPeak = peak
157	        let capMean = n > 0 ? sum / Double(n) : 0
158	        let capType = peakType
159	        let tvSignal = peakContext
160	        let tvLabel = peakContextLabel
161	        let ctx = contextAgg.sorted { $0.value > $1.value }.prefix(3)
162	            .map { ContextScore(label: $0.key, confidence: $0.value) }
163	        resetEpisode()
164	
165	        guard duration >= minDuration else { return }
166	
167	        // You-vs-TV hypothesis: a strong produced-audio context (soundtrack,
168	        // dialogue, audience, instruments) points at the TV; clean laughter with
169	        // little of that points at a person in the room.
170	        let origin: String
171	        let reason: String
172	        if tvSignal >= tvThreshold {
173	            origin = "tv"
174	            reason = String(format: "%@=%.2f (soundtrack/audience) → TV",
175	                            tvLabel.isEmpty ? "produced-audio" : tvLabel, tvSignal)
176	        } else {
177	            origin = "me"
178	            reason = String(format: "clean laughter, tv-context %.2f → you", tvSignal)
179	        }
180	
181	        let event = LaughEvent(start: s, end: end, duration: duration,
182	                               peak: capPeak, mean: capMean, type: capType,
183	                               context: ctx, origin: origin,
184	                               originReason: reason, tvSignal: tvSignal)
185	        if capPeak < countThreshold {
186	            if logCandidates { onCandidate?(event) }
187	        } else {
188	            onLaugh?(event)
189	        }
190	    }
191	
192	    private func resetEpisode() {
193	        start = nil; lastActive = 0; lastWindow = frameSeconds
194	        peak = 0; sum = 0; n = 0; peakType = ""
195	        peakContext = 0; peakContextLabel = ""; contextAgg = [:]
196	    }
197	}

=== README ===
# 😂 LaughCounter

**A thing that listens and counts the laughs.** LaughCounter runs quietly on the
always-on Mac mini in your living room, listens through a USB/webcam mic, detects
when you laugh, counts each laugh, notes *who* laughed (you vs. a guest), and logs
it — so you can see how much joy your days actually hold. It gets better over time
from a one-tap "I just laughed" whenever it misses one.

Everything runs locally. Your Google speaker keeps working as a Google speaker —
LaughCounter never touches it.

### ⬇️ Download

**[Get the latest macOS app → `LaughCounter.dmg`](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)** · [all releases](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases)

A ready-made build, published automatically on every change to `main` — no Xcode. See [`mac/README.md`](mac/README.md) to install.

---

## Two ways to run it

- **🍎 Native macOS app (recommended for the Mac mini)** — a tiny menu-bar app that
  uses macOS's **built-in** laughter detection, so there's **nothing to install**
  (no Python, no TensorFlow, no Homebrew) and nothing left behind when you delete
  it. Menu-bar count, a blip when a laugh is logged, and a hands-free "I just
  laughed" voice command. **⬇️ [Download the latest `LaughCounter.dmg`](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)**
  (a ready-made build from GitHub — no Xcode). **See [`mac/README.md`](mac/README.md).**
- **🐍 Python reference / simulator (this folder)** — a fully-tested,
  cross-platform implementation with a phone-friendly web dashboard, feedback
  commands, stats, and an offline `simulate` mode. Great for trying the whole
  pipeline anywhere. Documented below.

{"issues":[{"number":58,"title":"Remove the Python implementation","body":"Owner decision. The Python side (`laughcounter/`, ~2,100 lines across 17 modules, plus `tests/`) is a second, complete implementation of the product that nobody asked for.

Provenance, from git history:
- It was built **first** (`282b188`), before the native menu-bar app existed (`7ac1a72`).

It never runs: not shipped in the DMG, never invoked by the app, and no CI workflow executes it.

Scope: delete `laughcounter/`, `tests/`, and the packaging manifest; rewrite the README around the single native app; drop the design doc's §7 and Python-reference framing; remove Python entries from `.claudinite-checks.json`; and narrow the `on-device-privacy` pack to the Swift implementation (its `no-network-client` check scans both trees today, and its `RULES.md` describes the Python home directory and the optional-extra model download).

Accepted cost: the repo's only automated tests go with it (there are no Swift tests). The tests covered the Python counting/stats/storage logic, which the Swift app mirrors but does not share — so they never tested the shipping app.

**Finding**

`laughcounter/detector/robust.py:69`

```python
try:
    import laugh_segmenter  # noqa: F401  (provided by the repo)
    import torch  # noqa: F401
except ImportError as exc:  # pragma: no cover - depends on environment
    raise ImportError(_SETUP_HINT) from exc
```

`_SETUP_HINT` (module-level, line 30) re-raises without the phrase `pip install` anywhere in it, so a user who hits this from deep inside the detector gets a hint that talks about cloning a repo and setting `LAUGHCOUNTER_ROBUST_DIR`, but never spells out the exact `pip install ...` command for the pip-installable half of the dependency (`torch`; `laugh_segmenter` itself comes from the cloned checkout, not pip).

**Why it's flagged:** [`skills/python-optional-deps/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/skills/python-optional-deps/SKILL.md) — a guarded optional import that re-raises should carry an actionable `pip install pkg[extra]` hint naming the exact extra, not a bare/incomplete pointer.

**Why this needs a human call, not an automatic fix:** `robust`'s optional dependency isn't a simple pip extra — `torch` is pip-installable but `laugh_segmenter` requires cloning `jrgillick/laughter-detection` separately, so the "exact extra" the check wants named doesn't map cleanly onto a single `pip install pkg[extra]` command. Whether to add something like `pip install torch` alongside the existing clone/env-var instructions, restructure `_SETUP_HINT`, or leave it as-is (since the message already gives complete, accurate setup steps) is a judgment call for whoever owns this detector's UX.

Fix suggestion from the check: raise `ImportError` with a message naming the exact extra — e.g. `pip install "pkg[extra]"` — so the failure tells the user how to fix it.

This is advisory only (0 blocking findings this run) — no action required to keep CI green.

# LaughCounter for macOS (native menu-bar app)

The clean way to run LaughCounter on a Mac: a tiny menu-bar app that uses only
**built-in macOS frameworks** — nothing to install, nothing left behind.

- **Detects laughter** with Apple's built-in Sound Analysis (no model download).
- **Counts** distinct laughs and **logs** them to
  `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl` (no audio saved).
- **😄 menu-bar icon** shows today's count — that's your "it's running" light.
- **A soft blip** plays when a laugh is logged.
- **Say “I just laughed”** and it logs a laugh it missed, blipping **twice** to
  confirm (on-device speech recognition — nothing leaves your Mac). There's also a
  menu item / ⌘L if you'd rather click.

## Get it (no Xcode needed)

**⬇️ [Download the latest LaughCounter.dmg](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)** — this link always points at the most recent published release.

Prefer a specific build, or no release published yet? The app is also built for
every change by GitHub Actions on a macOS runner:

1. Go to the repo's **Actions** tab → open the latest **“Build macOS DMG”** run.
2. Download the **`LaughCounter-dmg`** artifact and unzip it to get `LaughCounter.dmg`.

*(Releases are published by pushing a `v*` tag — see “Cutting a release” below.)*

## Install

1. Open `LaughCounter.dmg` and drag **LaughCounter** into **Applications**.
2. **Get past Gatekeeper (first launch only).** The app is ad-hoc signed but not
   notarized (that needs a paid Apple Developer account), so macOS blocks the first
   open with *“Apple could not verify LaughCounter is free of malware.”* Clear it
   **one of two ways**:
   - **System Settings:** click **Done** on the warning, then open **System
     Settings → Privacy & Security**, scroll to **Security**, and click **Open
     Anyway** next to *“LaughCounter was blocked…”*. Confirm **Open Anyway** again.
   - **Terminal (most reliable):** after dragging it to Applications, run
     `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/LaughCounter.app`, then open it
     normally.

   > On **macOS 15 (Sequoia)** the old **right-click → Open** shortcut no longer
   > bypasses this — you must use one of the two methods above.
3. Approve **Microphone** and **Speech Recognition** when prompted.
4. A 😄 with a number appears in your menu bar. That's it.

**Always-on:** add it to **System Settings → General → Login Items** so it starts
with the Mac. **Uninstall:** quit it, drag the app to the Trash, and (optionally)
delete `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/`.

## Build it yourself (optional, on a Mac)

```bash
cd mac
python3 scripts/gen-icon.py   # -> Resources/AppIcon.png (only if you edit the icon)
bash scripts/build-app.sh     # -> dist/LaughCounter.app  (bakes AppIcon.icns)
bash scripts/make-dmg.sh      # -> dist/LaughCounter.dmg  (with the 😄 volume icon)
```

Requires the Swift toolchain (Xcode Command Line Tools). No third-party packages.
The app icon is generated from code by `scripts/gen-icon.py` (pure Python stdlib);
the committed `Resources/AppIcon.png` master is turned into a multi-resolution
`.icns` at build time with `sips`/`iconutil`.

This produces an **ad-hoc-signed** app (the Gatekeeper step under *Install*
applies). To instead sign it with a real **Developer ID** and notarize it — so it
opens with no warning — you need a paid Apple Developer account, then:

```bash
export MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)"
bash scripts/build-app.sh          # signs with Hardened Runtime + entitlements
bash scripts/make-dmg.sh
export APPLE_ID=you@example.com APPLE_TEAM_ID=XXXXXXXXXX APPLE_APP_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx
bash scripts/notarize-dmg.sh       # submits to Apple + staples the ticket
```

Both DMG workflows do this automatically when the matching repository secrets are
set (`MACOS_CERT_P12`, `MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD`, `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`,
`APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `APPLE_APP_PASSWORD`) — so published releases open with no
warning. This is the **non–App Store** path; a Mac App Store build additionally
requires the App Sandbox and a different (Apple Distribution) certificate.

## Cutting a release

Releases publish **automatically**. On every push to `main` that touches `mac/**`,
the **Release macOS DMG** workflow builds the app, packages the DMG, and
creates/updates the GitHub Release for the app's current version (read from
`Info.plist`), attaching `LaughCounter.dmg` — which is what the
[latest-release download link](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)
resolves to.

So to **ship a new version**, bump `CFBundleShortVersionString` in
`Resources/Info.plist` and merge to `main` — a new `v<version>` Release appears on
its own. (Merges that keep the same version just refresh that Release's DMG.) You
can also publish a Release from the GitHub UI, or run the workflow manually from
the Actions tab.

## The laugh log

Laughs are appended to `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl`,
one JSON object per line, fields in a fixed order:

| field | meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `start_iso` | human-readable start time (ISO-8601) |
| `label` | `auto` (detected), `missed` (you told us we missed one), `candidate` (sub-threshold — logged for tuning, **not counted**), `rejected` (not counted) |
| `start` / `end` | epoch seconds of the laugh's real start/end (from the classifier's window timing) |
| `peak` | highest laughter confidence during the laugh (0–1, rounded) |
| `duration` | `end − start` in seconds. **Coarse:** the built-in classifier analyses in ~3s windows, so a single laugh reads ~3s; only laughs spanning several windows read longer. It's a rough length, not a precise one. |
| `mean` | average laughter confidence across the laugh |
| `source` | `mic` (auto), `voice` (spoken “I just laughed”), `button` (menu / ⌘L) |
| `origin` | you-vs-TV **hypothesis**: `me` or `tv` |
| `tv_signal` | strongest produced-audio context (0–1) the hypothesis is based on |
| `origin_reason` | plain-language why (e.g. `music=0.66 (soundtrack/audience) → TV`) |
| `type` | which laugh class fired (e.g. giggle, chuckle), when known |
| `context` | top competing non-laugh classes heard |

**You vs the TV (two counters).** The menu bar shows `😄 N  📺 M` — your laughs vs
the TV's, today. Each laugh gets a *hypothesis*, not a verdict: a strong
produced-audio context (music, dialogue, audience, instruments — `tv_signal ≥ 0.3`)
is attributed to the TV; clean laughter with little of that is attributed to you.
Only *your* laughs blip. It will guess wrong sometimes (a real laugh over TV music),
which is why every laugh is still logged with its reasoning — nothing is discarded.
The class-based classifier can't hear *who* laughed; a loudness/proximity signal and,

**Sub-threshold logging:** anything that clears a deliberately low bar but not the

**Activity log:** lifecycle events (started / slept / woke / reconfigured / errors)
and each laugh's hypothesis go to `laughcounter.log` next to the laugh log (open it
from the menu), so if listening ever stops — or a guess looks off — you can see why.

## There is no "returned from standby" notification — fan in, then coalesce

macOS distinguishes sleep depths internally but exposes no standby-specific event:
`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires
several of them in a burst and each must not schedule its own restart:

- **Coalesce with an id, not a bool.** `pendingResumeID` holds the one in-flight
  resume; a stale timer compares its captured id and returns without touching
  state. A bare `resumePending` bool deadlocks: a re-sleep during the delay
  invalidates the timer, the timer clears the bool, and whichever of the two
  orderings loses leaves the next wake either unable to schedule (flag stuck true)
  or double-scheduling.
- **Gate on owing a resume**, i.e. `sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`.
  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
  three workspace triggers still cover the case.

## Resume by *intent*, and retry — a failed post-standby start has no second event

`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.

After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every
success / system return / manual resume. Bounded on purpose (a mic that is gone for
good emits nothing and must not be polled forever) and slow on purpose (rapid-cycling
is what wedges the mic). The wake settle is also stretched 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep
lasted longer than `standbyThreshold`; measure that span with `Date()`, **not**
`ProcessInfo.systemUptime`, which does not advance while the machine is asleep.

## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop

# macOS audio lifecycle — releasing the mic on every path

Hard-won rules for `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` (AudioHub, AppDelegate's restart
machinery, VoiceCommand). Read before touching engine start/stop, sleep/wake, or
exit handling.

**The invariant.** If this process ends — or intentionally stops capture — while
the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
overlap restarts. (#22)

## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself

`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal

`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a

all future starts.

input.title: Reactivate the counter when the Mac returns from standby
input.body:
Detects the Mac coming back from standby and switches the left counter (`😄 N`, i.e. listening) back on — **only if it was active before**.

## Why the existing wake handling wasn't enough

`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` was already observed, but three things were missing for standby specifically:

1. **A wake is not always a return.** A dark / Power-Nap wake fires `didWake` with nobody there and the Mac re-sleeps moments later — macOS exposes no standby-specific event to tell them apart.
2. **It resumed unconditionally.** Whatever the state before sleep, waking restarted capture.
3. **A failed post-standby start was terminal.** After a long standby the USB bus was powered down, so the mic is often still re-enumerating when the 1.0s settle window closes. That start throws — and unlike the config-change cases, *nothing else ever fires* to recover from it, so the app sat silently "not listening" until someone opened the menu.

## What changed (`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/AppDelegate.swift`)

**Fan in the return signals, then coalesce.** `didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive` and the distributed `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` all funnel into one `systemDidReturn(reason:)`. A real return fires several in a burst, so the resume is coalesced behind `pendingResumeID` — an id, not a bool: a bool deadlocks when a re-sleep invalidates the timer and the timer then clears the flag. Later signals act as backstops if the first resume didn't get the counter running. Guarded on actually owing a resume (`sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`), so a screensaver dismissal or a user switch never cycles a healthy engine — that's the mic-wedge condition from #22.

**Resume by intent.** New `listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is distinct from `listening` ("the engine actually is"). Sleep suspends capture without clearing the intent, so a return reactivates only a counter that was active before; a start that merely *failed* keeps the intent and stays eligible for recovery. Branching on `listening` instead would have made any pre-sleep failure permanent. Today the intent is false only when the microphone was never granted or before the first start — there is no user-facing pause yet (happy to add one if you want the conditional to be reachable by hand).

**Give the hardware time, then retry.** The settle stretches 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep lasted past `standbyThreshold` (5 min), measured with `Date()` — `ProcessInfo.systemUptime` does not advance while asleep. On top of that, `scheduleStartRetry` backs off 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s → 32s, five attempts, then gives up with an ERROR line pointing at the menu. Bounded because a mic that is gone for good emits nothing and must not be polled forever; slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic. Generation-guarded like every other deferred restart, and reset on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume.

Every new deferred closure follows the existing invariants: generation-guarded, main-thread only, and the resume timer always ungates `sleeping` — including on the "stay off" path, or the menu's Start item would be blocked forever.

## Docs

- `mac/README.md` — a *Sleep & standby* note on what users should expect.
- `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` — two new sections: the no-standby-event fan-in/coalesce rules, and resume-by-intent plus why the retry ladder exists.

## Testing

**Not built or run — no Swift toolchain in this Linux session, and the sleep/standby paths need real hardware anyway.** The Claudinite work checks pass (`check_the_work.mjs`, exit 0). The DMG workflow on this branch is the first actual compile; worth confirming it's green before merging, and then a real check on the Mac mini: sleep it past 5 minutes, wake, and confirm the activity log shows `system woke after Ns standby — resuming listening shortly` followed by `listening started`.

reactivate the counter when the Mac returns from standby

macOS exposes no "returned from standby" event — only the ordinary
NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification, which also fires for dark/Power-Nap wakes
where nobody is there and the machine re-sleeps at once. Fan the wake in
with screensDidWake, sessionDidBecomeActive and the distributed
com.apple.screenIsUnlocked, and coalesce the burst into a single resume
identified by an id (a bare bool deadlocks when a re-sleep races the timer).

Resume by intent, not by engine state: `listeningIntent` records that the
counter is meant to be running, so a return reactivates only a counter that
was actually active before the Mac went down — while a start that merely
failed stays eligible for recovery, which branching on `listening` would
have made permanent.

After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
re-enumerating when the settle window closes; that start throws and nothing
else ever fires to recover from it, leaving the app silently not listening.
So stretch the settle 1.0s → 2.5s for sleeps past the standby threshold, and
add a bounded retry ladder (2s → 32s, five attempts, generation-guarded)
that resets on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume. Bounded
because a mic that is gone emits nothing and must not be polled forever;
slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic.

Documents the behaviour in mac/README.md and the reasoning in
dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md.

lastPrompt: Can you add some trigger for detecting when the computer returns from standby? And in case the left counter was active before, reactivate it.

content.text: The macOS DMG build passed on this commit — so it does compile. Updating the PR's stale testing note:

input.body:
Detects the Mac coming back from standby and switches the left counter (`😄 N`, i.e. listening) back on — **only if it was active before**.

## Why the existing wake handling wasn't enough

`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` was already observed, but three things were missing for standby specifically:

1. **A wake is not always a return.** A dark / Power-Nap wake fires `didWake` with nobody there and the Mac re-sleeps moments later — macOS exposes no standby-specific event to tell them apart.
2. **It resumed unconditionally.** Whatever the state before sleep, waking restarted capture.
3. **A failed post-standby start was terminal.** After a long standby the USB bus was powered down, so the mic is often still re-enumerating when the 1.0s settle window closes. That start throws — and unlike the config-change cases, *nothing else ever fires* to recover from it, so the app sat silently "not listening" until someone opened the menu.

## What changed (`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/AppDelegate.swift`)

**Fan in the return signals, then coalesce.** `didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive` and the distributed `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` all funnel into one `systemDidReturn(reason:)`. A real return fires several in a burst, so the resume is coalesced behind `pendingResumeID` — an id, not a bool: a bool deadlocks when a re-sleep invalidates the timer and the timer then clears the flag. Later signals act as backstops if the first resume didn't get the counter running. Guarded on actually owing a resume (`sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`), so a screensaver dismissal or a user switch never cycles a healthy engine — that's the mic-wedge condition from #22.

**Resume by intent.** New `listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is distinct from `listening` ("the engine actually is"). Sleep suspends capture without clearing the intent, so a return reactivates only a counter that was active before; a start that merely *failed* keeps the intent and stays eligible for recovery. Branching on `listening` instead would have made any pre-sleep failure permanent. Today the intent is false only when the microphone was never granted or before the first start — there is no user-facing pause yet (happy to add one if you want the conditional to be reachable by hand).

**Give the hardware time, then retry.** The settle stretches 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep lasted past `standbyThreshold` (5 min), measured with `Date()` — `ProcessInfo.systemUptime` does not advance while asleep. On top of that, `scheduleStartRetry` backs off 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s → 32s, five attempts, then gives up with an ERROR line pointing at the menu. Bounded because a mic that is gone for good emits nothing and must not be polled forever; slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic. Generation-guarded like every other deferred restart, and reset on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume.

Every new deferred closure follows the existing invariants: generation-guarded, main-thread only, and the resume timer always ungates `sleeping` — including on the "stay off" path, or the menu's Start item would be blocked forever.

## Docs

- `mac/README.md` — a *Sleep & standby* note on what users should expect.
- `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` — two new sections: the no-standby-event fan-in/coalesce rules, and resume-by-intent plus why the retry ladder exists.

## Testing

- **Compiles:** the Build macOS DMG workflow is green on `52f0ab1` ([run](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/actions/runs/30379715753)). That is the only automated coverage — the repo has no Swift tests, and this session runs on Linux with no Swift toolchain.
- **Not exercised on hardware.** The sleep/standby paths need a real Mac. Worth a check on the Mac mini: sleep it past 5 minutes, wake it, and confirm the activity log shows `system woke after Ns standby — resuming listening shortly` followed by `listening started`. Unplugging the USB mic across the sleep exercises the retry ladder.

**How I read "left counter":** the `😄 N` half of the menu-bar title (`mac/README.md` calls those "two counters" — yours vs the TV's). Both counters are fed by the one mic engine, so "reactivate it" = resume listening.

**What was already there:** `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` resumed listening 1s after any wake, unconditionally.

**What I added** (`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/AppDelegate.swift:369`):

- **A wider standby trigger.** macOS has no "returned from standby" event — standby is just a deeper sleep, and a bare `didWake` also fires for dark/Power-Nap wakes with nobody there. So `didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive` and the distributed `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` all funnel into one `systemDidReturn(reason:)`, coalesced behind an id so the burst schedules a single resume — the later ones acting as backstops. It only reacts when a resume is actually owed, so a screensaver dismissal never cycles a healthy engine (the USB-mic wedge condition from #22).
- **Conditional reactivation.** New `listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is separate from `listening` ("the engine is"). Sleep suspends without clearing it, so a return switches the counter back on only if it was on. One nuance I deliberately kept: a start that merely *failed* keeps the intent, so it stays eligible for recovery — branching on `listening` would have made any pre-sleep failure permanent.
- **A retry ladder**, because a resume that fails isn't a reactivation. After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic is often still re-enumerating when the settle window closes; that start throws and nothing else ever fires to recover. The settle stretches 1.0s → 2.5s past a 5-minute sleep, then retries back off 2s → 32s, five attempts, then gives up with a log line. Bounded and slow on purpose.

Docs: a *Sleep & standby* note in `mac/README.md`, and the reasoning in `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` as the local canon requires.

**Verification:** the Build macOS DMG workflow is green on the commit, so it compiles — that's the only automated coverage (no Swift tests exist, and this container is Linux with no toolchain). The sleep paths themselves need the real Mac mini.

One thing worth your call: today `listeningIntent` is false only when the mic was never granted, since there's no user-facing pause — so the "was it active?" condition rarely bites. Say the word and I'll add a **Pause listening** menu item so it's reachable by hand.

> ⚠️ Still open: hardware check on the Mac mini (sleep >5 min, wake, expect `system woke after Ns standby — resuming listening shortly` → `listening started`), and your decision on the Pause menu item. Want me to watch #59 for CI and review comments?
