input.title: Reactivate the counter when the Mac returns from standby
input.body:
Owner request: detect when the Mac comes back from standby, and if the left counter (`😄 N` — listening) was active before, switch it back on.

The app already observes `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` and resumes 1s later, but three things are missing for standby specifically:

1. **A wake is not always a return.** macOS exposes no standby-specific event — standby is just a deeper sleep — and a bare `didWake` also fires for dark / Power-Nap wakes where nobody is there and the machine re-sleeps at once.
2. **The resume is unconditional.** Whatever the state before sleep, waking restarts capture; it should reactivate only a counter that was actually active.
3. **A failed post-standby start is terminal.** After a long standby the USB bus was powered down, so the mic is often still re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and unlike the config-change cases nothing else ever fires to recover from it — the app then sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu.

Scope: fan the wake in with the other "the machine is back" signals and coalesce them into a single resume; branch the resume on a "the counter is meant to be running" intent rather than on the engine's live state; and give the hardware proportionally longer after a long sleep, with a bounded, backing-off retry so a slow mic still ends up listening. All within the `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` lifecycle invariants (release the mic on every path, never rapid-cycle or overlap restarts — #22).

Out of scope for now: a user-facing **Pause listening** menu item. Without one, the "was it active?" condition is only reachable via microphone permission being denied.

Implemented by PR #59.

reactivate the counter when the Mac returns from standby

macOS exposes no "returned from standby" event — only the ordinary
NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification, which also fires for dark/Power-Nap wakes
where nobody is there and the machine re-sleeps at once. Fan the wake in
with screensDidWake, sessionDidBecomeActive and the distributed
com.apple.screenIsUnlocked, and coalesce the burst into a single resume
identified by an id (a bare bool deadlocks when a re-sleep races the timer).

Resume by intent, not by engine state: `listeningIntent` records that the
counter is meant to be running, so a return reactivates only a counter that
was actually active before the Mac went down — while a start that merely
failed stays eligible for recovery, which branching on `listening` would
have made permanent.

After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
re-enumerating when the settle window closes; that start throws and nothing
else ever fires to recover from it, leaving the app silently not listening.
So stretch the settle 1.0s → 2.5s for sleeps past the standby threshold, and
add a bounded retry ladder (2s → 32s, five attempts, generation-guarded)
that resets on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume. Bounded
because a mic that is gone emits nothing and must not be polled forever;
slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic.

Documents the behaviour in mac/README.md and the reasoning in
dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md.

input.body:
Closes #60.

Detects the Mac coming back from standby and switches the left counter (`😄 N`, i.e. listening) back on — **only if it was active before**.

## Why the existing wake handling wasn't enough

`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` was already observed, but three things were missing for standby specifically:

1. **A wake is not always a return.** A dark / Power-Nap wake fires `didWake` with nobody there and the Mac re-sleeps moments later — macOS exposes no standby-specific event to tell them apart.
2. **It resumed unconditionally.** Whatever the state before sleep, waking restarted capture.
3. **A failed post-standby start was terminal.** After a long standby the USB bus was powered down, so the mic is often still re-enumerating when the 1.0s settle window closes. That start throws — and unlike the config-change cases, *nothing else ever fires* to recover from it, so the app sat silently "not listening" until someone opened the menu.

## What changed (`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/AppDelegate.swift`)

**Fan in the return signals, then coalesce.** `didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive` and the distributed `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` all funnel into one `systemDidReturn(reason:)`. A real return fires several in a burst, so the resume is coalesced behind `pendingResumeID` — an id, not a bool: a bool deadlocks when a re-sleep invalidates the timer and the timer then clears the flag. Later signals act as backstops if the first resume didn't get the counter running. Guarded on actually owing a resume (`sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`), so a screensaver dismissal or a user switch never cycles a healthy engine — that's the mic-wedge condition from #22.

**Resume by intent.** New `listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is distinct from `listening` ("the engine actually is"). Sleep suspends capture without clearing the intent, so a return reactivates only a counter that was active before; a start that merely *failed* keeps the intent and stays eligible for recovery. Branching on `listening` instead would have made any pre-sleep failure permanent. Today the intent is false only when the microphone was never granted or before the first start — there is no user-facing pause yet (happy to add one if you want the conditional to be reachable by hand).

**Give the hardware time, then retry.** The settle stretches 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep lasted past `standbyThreshold` (5 min), measured with `Date()` — `ProcessInfo.systemUptime` does not advance while asleep. On top of that, `scheduleStartRetry` backs off 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s → 32s, five attempts, then gives up with an ERROR line pointing at the menu. Bounded because a mic that is gone for good emits nothing and must not be polled forever; slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic. Generation-guarded like every other deferred restart, and reset on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume.

Every new deferred closure follows the existing invariants: generation-guarded, main-thread only, and the resume timer always ungates `sleeping` — including on the "stay off" path, or the menu's Start item would be blocked forever.

## Docs

- `mac/README.md` — a *Sleep & standby* note on what users should expect.
- `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` — two new sections: the no-standby-event fan-in/coalesce rules, and resume-by-intent plus why the retry ladder exists.

## Testing

- **Compiles:** the Build macOS DMG workflow went green on this tree ([run 25](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/actions/runs/30379715753); the commit was then amended to reference #60, leaving the tree byte-identical, and [run 26](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/actions/runs/30380287231) rebuilds it). That is the only automated coverage — the repo has no Swift tests, and this session runs on Linux with no Swift toolchain.
- **Not exercised on hardware.** The sleep/standby paths need a real Mac. Worth a check on the Mac mini: sleep it past 5 minutes, wake it, and confirm the activity log shows `system woke after Ns standby — resuming listening shortly` followed by `listening started`. Unplugging the USB mic across the sleep exercises the retry ladder.

reactivate the counter when the Mac returns from standby

macOS exposes no "returned from standby" event — only the ordinary
NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification, which also fires for dark/Power-Nap wakes
where nobody is there and the machine re-sleeps at once. Fan the wake in
with screensDidWake, sessionDidBecomeActive and the distributed
com.apple.screenIsUnlocked, and coalesce the burst into a single resume
identified by an id (a bare bool deadlocks when a re-sleep races the timer).

Resume by intent, not by engine state: `listeningIntent` records that the
counter is meant to be running, so a return reactivates only a counter that
was actually active before the Mac went down — while a start that merely
failed stays eligible for recovery, which branching on `listening` would
have made permanent.

After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
re-enumerating when the settle window closes; that start throws and nothing
else ever fires to recover from it, leaving the app silently not listening.
So stretch the settle 1.0s → 2.5s for sleeps past the standby threshold, and
add a bounded retry ladder (2s → 32s, five attempts, generation-guarded)
that resets on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume. Bounded
because a mic that is gone emits nothing and must not be polled forever;
slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic.

Documents the behaviour in mac/README.md and the reasoning in
dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md.

content.text:
Comment class: feature

Both blocking findings from the conformance check are fixed:

- **Issue created** — [#60](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/issues/60), capturing the request and the three gaps in the existing wake handling; the commit now ends `Closes #60` (amended and force-pushed with `--force-with-lease`).
- **Classification** — stated above.

CI is green on the new head `aaec488` ([run 26](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/actions/runs/30380287231)), and `check_the_work.mjs` exits 0.

**[PR #59](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/pull/59)** — reactivate the counter when the Mac returns from standby:

- `didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive` and the distributed `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` fan into one `systemDidReturn(reason:)`, coalesced behind an id so a return's burst schedules a single resume, with the later signals as backstops. macOS has no standby-specific event, and a bare `didWake` also fires for dark/Power-Nap wakes with nobody there.
- New `listeningIntent` makes the resume conditional: sleep suspends without clearing it, so a return switches the counter back on only if it was on. A start that merely *failed* keeps the intent, so it stays recoverable.
- Settle stretches 1.0s → 2.5s past a 5-minute sleep, plus a bounded retry ladder (2s → 32s, five attempts, generation-guarded) for the post-standby case where the USB mic is still re-enumerating — previously that failure was terminal.
- Docs: *Sleep & standby* in `mac/README.md`; the reasoning in `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md`.

> ⚠️ Still open — nothing blocking, but two things need you:
> - **Hardware check on the Mac mini** (the sleep paths can't be exercised here): sleep >5 min, wake, expect `system woke after Ns standby — resuming listening shortly` → `listening started`. Unplugging the mic across the sleep exercises the retry ladder.
> - **Your call on a "Pause listening" menu item** — without one, `listeningIntent` is false only when the mic was never granted, so the "was it active?" condition rarely bites. Say the word and I'll add it.
>
> Want me to watch #59 for CI and review comments?

# LaughCounter for macOS (native menu-bar app)

The clean way to run LaughCounter on a Mac: a tiny menu-bar app that uses only
**built-in macOS frameworks** — nothing to install, nothing left behind.

- **Detects laughter** with Apple's built-in Sound Analysis (no model download).
- **Counts** distinct laughs and **logs** them to
  `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl` (no audio saved).
- **😄 menu-bar icon** shows today's count — that's your "it's running" light.
- **A soft blip** plays when a laugh is logged.
- **Say “I just laughed”** and it logs a laugh it missed, blipping **twice** to
  confirm (on-device speech recognition — nothing leaves your Mac). There's also a
  menu item / ⌘L if you'd rather click.

## Get it (no Xcode needed)

**⬇️ [Download the latest LaughCounter.dmg](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)** — this link always points at the most recent published release.

Prefer a specific build, or no release published yet? The app is also built for
every change by GitHub Actions on a macOS runner:

1. Go to the repo's **Actions** tab → open the latest **“Build macOS DMG”** run.
2. Download the **`LaughCounter-dmg`** artifact and unzip it to get `LaughCounter.dmg`.

*(Releases are published by pushing a `v*` tag — see “Cutting a release” below.)*

## Install

1. Open `LaughCounter.dmg` and drag **LaughCounter** into **Applications**.
2. **Get past Gatekeeper (first launch only).** The app is ad-hoc signed but not
   notarized (that needs a paid Apple Developer account), so macOS blocks the first
   open with *“Apple could not verify LaughCounter is free of malware.”* Clear it
   **one of two ways**:
   - **System Settings:** click **Done** on the warning, then open **System
     Settings → Privacy & Security**, scroll to **Security**, and click **Open
     Anyway** next to *“LaughCounter was blocked…”*. Confirm **Open Anyway** again.
   - **Terminal (most reliable):** after dragging it to Applications, run
     `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/LaughCounter.app`, then open it
     normally.

   > On **macOS 15 (Sequoia)** the old **right-click → Open** shortcut no longer
   > bypasses this — you must use one of the two methods above.
3. Approve **Microphone** and **Speech Recognition** when prompted.
4. A 😄 with a number appears in your menu bar. That's it.

**Always-on:** add it to **System Settings → General → Login Items** so it starts
with the Mac. **Uninstall:** quit it, drag the app to the Trash, and (optionally)
delete `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/`.

## Build it yourself (optional, on a Mac)

```bash
cd mac
python3 scripts/gen-icon.py   # -> Resources/AppIcon.png (only if you edit the icon)
bash scripts/build-app.sh     # -> dist/LaughCounter.app  (bakes AppIcon.icns)
bash scripts/make-dmg.sh      # -> dist/LaughCounter.dmg  (with the 😄 volume icon)
```

Requires the Swift toolchain (Xcode Command Line Tools). No third-party packages.
The app icon is generated from code by `scripts/gen-icon.py` (pure Python stdlib);
the committed `Resources/AppIcon.png` master is turned into a multi-resolution
`.icns` at build time with `sips`/`iconutil`.

This produces an **ad-hoc-signed** app (the Gatekeeper step under *Install*
applies). To instead sign it with a real **Developer ID** and notarize it — so it
opens with no warning — you need a paid Apple Developer account, then:

```bash
export MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)"
bash scripts/build-app.sh          # signs with Hardened Runtime + entitlements
bash scripts/make-dmg.sh
export APPLE_ID=you@example.com APPLE_TEAM_ID=XXXXXXXXXX APPLE_APP_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx
bash scripts/notarize-dmg.sh       # submits to Apple + staples the ticket
```

Both DMG workflows do this automatically when the matching repository secrets are
set (`MACOS_CERT_P12`, `MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD`, `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`,
`APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `APPLE_APP_PASSWORD`) — so published releases open with no
warning. This is the **non–App Store** path; a Mac App Store build additionally
requires the App Sandbox and a different (Apple Distribution) certificate.

## Cutting a release

Releases publish **automatically**. On every push to `main` that touches `mac/**`,
the **Release macOS DMG** workflow builds the app, packages the DMG, and
creates/updates the GitHub Release for the app's current version (read from
`Info.plist`), attaching `LaughCounter.dmg` — which is what the
[latest-release download link](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)
resolves to.

So to **ship a new version**, bump `CFBundleShortVersionString` in
`Resources/Info.plist` and merge to `main` — a new `v<version>` Release appears on
its own. (Merges that keep the same version just refresh that Release's DMG.) You
can also publish a Release from the GitHub UI, or run the workflow manually from
the Actions tab.

## The laugh log

Laughs are appended to `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl`,
one JSON object per line, fields in a fixed order:

| field | meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `start_iso` | human-readable start time (ISO-8601) |
| `label` | `auto` (detected), `missed` (you told us we missed one), `candidate` (sub-threshold — logged for tuning, **not counted**), `rejected` (not counted) |
| `start` / `end` | epoch seconds of the laugh's real start/end (from the classifier's window timing) |
| `peak` | highest laughter confidence during the laugh (0–1, rounded) |
| `duration` | `end − start` in seconds. **Coarse:** the built-in classifier analyses in ~3s windows, so a single laugh reads ~3s; only laughs spanning several windows read longer. It's a rough length, not a precise one. |
| `mean` | average laughter confidence across the laugh |
| `source` | `mic` (auto), `voice` (spoken “I just laughed”), `button` (menu / ⌘L) |
| `origin` | you-vs-TV **hypothesis**: `me` or `tv` |
| `tv_signal` | strongest produced-audio context (0–1) the hypothesis is based on |
| `origin_reason` | plain-language why (e.g. `music=0.66 (soundtrack/audience) → TV`) |
| `type` | which laugh class fired (e.g. giggle, chuckle), when known |
| `context` | top competing non-laugh classes heard |

**You vs the TV (two counters).** The menu bar shows `😄 N  📺 M` — your laughs vs
the TV's, today. Each laugh gets a *hypothesis*, not a verdict: a strong
produced-audio context (music, dialogue, audience, instruments — `tv_signal ≥ 0.3`)
is attributed to the TV; clean laughter with little of that is attributed to you.
Only *your* laughs blip. It will guess wrong sometimes (a real laugh over TV music),
which is why every laugh is still logged with its reasoning — nothing is discarded.
The class-based classifier can't hear *who* laughed; a loudness/proximity signal and,
eventually, laugh enrollment would sharpen it.

**Sub-threshold logging:** anything that clears a deliberately low bar but not the
counting threshold is written with `label:"candidate"` (uncounted) — so near-misses
are on record and later “I laughed” feedback can be aligned to a nearby event.

**Sleep & standby:** the mic is released when the Mac sleeps and picked back up
when it returns — from a short sleep or from a long standby, where the USB bus was
powered down and the mic takes a while to reappear (LaughCounter waits longer, then
retries with a widening gap for about a minute before giving up and telling you so
in the activity log). It resumes **only if the counter was running when the Mac went
to sleep**: if listening was off — say the microphone was never granted — waking the
Mac leaves it off. A wake with nobody there (Power Nap, a screensaver dismissed)
doesn't restart anything that was already running.

**Activity log:** lifecycle events (started / slept / woke / reconfigured / errors)
and each laugh's hypothesis go to `laughcounter.log` next to the laugh log (open it
from the menu), so if listening ever stops — or a guess looks off — you can see why.

## Notes & limits

See [`../docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md`](../docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md) for the
full picture: how misses become improvements (threshold tuning now, a personalised
Create ML model later), the who-laughed plan, and the voice-command tradeoffs
(false triggers, on-device availability).

# macOS audio lifecycle — releasing the mic on every path

Hard-won rules for `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` (AudioHub, AppDelegate's restart
machinery, VoiceCommand). Read before touching engine start/stop, sleep/wake, or
exit handling.

**The invariant.** If this process ends — or intentionally stops capture — while
the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
overlap restarts. (#22)

## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself

`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal
default. SIGKILL/Force-Quit/crash remain uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug.
Don't add `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` to Info.plist: it would let logout
SIGKILL the app past all of this.

## Deferred work must be generation-guarded

`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or
un-settled at wake. Every intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every
delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.
When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /
`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
all future starts.

## There is no "returned from standby" notification — fan in, then coalesce

macOS distinguishes sleep depths internally but exposes no standby-specific event:
`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires
several of them in a burst and each must not schedule its own restart:

- **Coalesce with an id, not a bool.** `pendingResumeID` holds the one in-flight
  resume; a stale timer compares its captured id and returns without touching
  state. A bare `resumePending` bool deadlocks: a re-sleep during the delay
  invalidates the timer, the timer clears the bool, and whichever of the two
  orderings loses leaves the next wake either unable to schedule (flag stuck true)
  or double-scheduling.
- **Gate on owing a resume**, i.e. `sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`.
  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
  three workspace triggers still cover the case.

## Resume by *intent*, and retry — a failed post-standby start has no second event

`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.

After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every
success / system return / manual resume. Bounded on purpose (a mic that is gone for
good emits nothing and must not be polled forever) and slow on purpose (rapid-cycling
is what wedges the mic). The wake settle is also stretched 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep

input.body:
Closes #60.

Detects the Mac coming back from standby and switches the left counter (`😄 N`, i.e. listening) back on — **only if it was active before**.

## Why the existing wake handling wasn't enough

`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` was already observed, but three things were missing for standby specifically:

1. **A wake is not always a return.** A dark / Power-Nap wake fires `didWake` with nobody there and the Mac re-sleeps moments later — macOS exposes no standby-specific event to tell them apart.
2. **It resumed unconditionally.** Whatever the state before sleep, waking restarted capture.
3. **A failed post-standby start was terminal.** After a long standby the USB bus was powered down, so the mic is often still re-enumerating when the 1.0s settle window closes. That start throws — and unlike the config-change cases, *nothing else ever fires* to recover from it, so the app sat silently "not listening" until someone opened the menu.

## What changed (`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/AppDelegate.swift`)

**Fan in the return signals, then coalesce.** `didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive` and the distributed `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` all funnel into one `systemDidReturn(reason:)`. A real return fires several in a burst, so the resume is coalesced behind `pendingResumeID` — an id, not a bool: a bool deadlocks when a re-sleep invalidates the timer and the timer then clears the flag. Later signals act as backstops if the first resume didn't get the counter running. Guarded on actually owing a resume (`sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`), so a screensaver dismissal or a user switch never cycles a healthy engine — that's the mic-wedge condition from #22.

**Resume by intent.** The counter's "meant to be running" state is held as `offReason: String?` (nil = running), distinct from `listening` ("the engine actually is"). Sleep suspends capture without touching it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was active before; a start that merely *failed* keeps the intent and stays eligible for recovery. Branching on `listening` instead would have made any pre-sleep failure permanent. One field rather than a bool beside a separate reason string, so the menu status, the tooltip and the wake log can't disagree about whether the counter is off or why.

**Pause listening (⌘P).** Makes that condition reachable by hand — previously the intent was false only when the microphone was denied. Releases the mic until *Start listening* is picked again; the menu reads `Status: paused`. Not persisted (relaunching starts listening, which is what an always-on box should do after a power cut), and sleeping while paused comes back paused.

**Give the hardware time, then retry.** The settle stretches 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep lasted past `standbyThreshold` (5 min), measured with `Date()` — `ProcessInfo.systemUptime` does not advance while asleep. On top of that, `scheduleStartRetry` backs off 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s → 32s, five attempts, then gives up with an ERROR line pointing at the menu. Bounded because a mic that is gone for good emits nothing and must not be polled forever; slow because rapid-cycling is what wedges a USB mic. Generation-guarded like every other deferred restart, and reset on success, on a system return, and on a manual resume.

Every new deferred closure follows the existing invariants: generation-guarded, main-thread only, and the resume timer always ungates `sleeping` — including on the "stay off" path, or the menu's Start item would be blocked forever.

## Docs

- `mac/README.md` — *Pause* and *Sleep & standby* notes on what users should expect.
- `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` — the no-standby-event fan-in/coalesce rules, resume-by-intent (and why the intent is one field), and why the retry ladder exists.

## Testing

- **Compiles:** the Build macOS DMG workflow is the only automated coverage — the repo has no Swift tests, and this session runs on Linux with no Swift toolchain.
- **Not exercised on hardware.** Two of the constants here are estimates rather than measurements: the 5-minute standby threshold and the 2.5s post-standby settle. Diagnostics are being gathered from the real Mac mini (power settings, `pmset -g log` wake types and durations, and whether the *current* build's activity log shows post-wake `could not start listening` failures) before either is treated as final.

content.text:
Comment class: feature

**Pause listening (⌘P) is in** — [PR #59](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/pull/59), commit `9775e9e`. It releases the mic until *Start listening* is picked again, the menu reads `Status: paused`, and sleeping while paused comes back paused. I folded the intent into one field (`offReason: String?` — nil means "meant to be running") so the menu, tooltip and wake log can't disagree about whether the counter is off or *why*: `paused`, `no microphone access`, `starting up`.

And yes — logs would help. Two constants in this PR are estimates, not measurements, and your machine is the only thing that can settle them. **No more code until these come back.**

### Run any time — one snapshot file

```bash
{
  echo "=== now ==="; date
  echo; echo "=== pmset -g (live) ==="; pmset -g
  echo; echo "=== pmset -g custom ==="; pmset -g custom
  echo; echo "=== pmset -g assertions ==="; pmset -g assertions
  echo; echo "=== sleep/wake history ==="
  pmset -g log | grep -E "^[0-9]{4}-.*(Sleep|Wake|Standby|Hibernate)" | tail -150
  echo; echo "=== audio devices ==="; system_profiler SPAudioDataType
  echo; echo "=== USB devices ==="; system_profiler SPUSBDataType
  echo; echo "=== screen lock ==="
  defaults -currentHost read com.apple.screensaver askForPassword 2>&1
  echo; echo "=== LaughCounter activity log ==="
  tail -n 300 "$HOME/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log" 2>&1
} > ~/Desktop/laughcounter-diag.txt 2>&1
echo "wrote ~/Desktop/laughcounter-diag.txt"
```

Takes ~30s (`pmset -g log` is slow on a long-running machine). Paste the file back — it's all local config and LaughCounter's own log, no laugh contents.

### Then, right after the next real wake

Wake the Mac after it's been asleep a while (overnight is ideal) and run this within a few seconds:

```bash
s=$(date +%s)
for i in $(seq 1 25); do
  printf '%3ds  input-capable devices: %s\n' "$(( $(date +%s) - s ))" \
    "$(system_profiler SPAudioDataType 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'Input Channels')"
done | tee ~/Desktop/mic-return.txt
tail -n 40 "$HOME/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log"
```

### What each answers

| Question | Read from | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Does the mini sleep at all, and does it reach standby/hibernate? | `pmset -g`, `pmset -g custom` | If `sleep 0`, this whole path is dormant and the PR is insurance, not a fix |
| Are there **DarkWakes** (Power Nap / maintenance), or only real wakes? | sleep/wake history | The premise behind fanning in the extra triggers. If the mini never dark-wakes, that part is belt-and-braces |
| How long is it typically asleep? | sleep/wake history timestamps | Sets the standby threshold — I guessed **5 min**, which is a guess |
| **Does the current build already fail to restart after a wake?** | activity log — `could not start listening: microphone input format not ready` right after `system woke` | The load-bearing one. If those failures are in there, the retry ladder is the actual fix; if every wake goes straight to `listening started`, 2.5s is plenty and the ladder is just a safety net |
| How many seconds until the mic is really back? | `mic-return.txt` | Sets the post-standby settle — I guessed **2.5s** |
| USB mic or built-in/HDMI? | audio + USB device lists | The wedge and the slow re-enumeration are USB-specific |
| Does the screen actually lock? | screen lock setting | If it never locks, `com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` never fires and the other three triggers carry it |

One caveat on reading the activity log: it comes from the **currently installed** build, which resumes unconditionally 1.0s after any wake. That's exactly what makes it useful — it's the unpatched baseline.

> ⚠️ Waiting on you: the two files above. Once I see them I'll either confirm the 5-min / 2.5s constants or tune them to what the machine actually does — and if the log shows a failure mode I didn't anticipate, better to find it now than after a deploy.

content.text:
Comment class: correction

**First, a correction to my read.** The grep I gave you was too greedy — assertion lines contain the word "Sleep", so `tail -150` filled up with those and cut off the actual sleep/wake events. I can't conclude the Mac never slept. (`sleep 0` only disables *idle* sleep; a manual or scheduled sleep still happens, which fits what you're telling me.) The script below filters those out properly.

**What does stand, from LaughCounter's own log:** three times, the app logged `audio configuration changed — reconfiguring` and then went **completely silent** — no `listening started`, no `could not start listening`, nothing — until you launched it by hand.

| local time | LaughCounter log | what the system was doing |
|---|---|---|
| Jul 13, 00:52 | `audio configuration changed` → **silence for 15 days** | — |
| Jul 28, 16:25 | `app launched` → `listening started` | (hand launch) |
| Jul 28, 17:38:33 | | display sleeps (powerd drops "prevent sleep while display is on") |
| Jul 28, 17:38:52 | `audio configuration changed` → **silence** | coreaudiod tears down ~25 audio contexts |
| Jul 28, 19:35:38 | `app launched` → `listening started` | (hand launch) |
| Jul 28, 19:36:10 | `audio configuration changed` → **silence** | coreaudiod tears down the **Logitech BRIO** engine |
| Jul 28, 19:43 | | BRIO reappears on USB (~7 min gone) |
| Jul 28, 20:33 | still silent (~1h) | you ran the diagnostics |

Two of the three deaths line up to the *second* with coreaudiod tearing down audio contexts. So the trigger is real and reproducible — but it's an audio-device event, not a wake.

The decisive unknown: **did the app crash, or is it alive with a wedged restart latch?** In the current code there are exactly two exits that log nothing — a crash (the `installTap` uncatchable NSException the code already warns about), or `requestListening` returning early on a stuck `restartInFlight`. `pgrep` alone separates them, and the crash reports settle it. All retrospective — run it now:

```bash
OUT=~/Desktop/laughcounter-diag2.txt
LOG="$HOME/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log"
{
  echo "=== now ==="; date
  echo; echo "=== is LaughCounter running? ==="
  if pgrep -x LaughCounter >/dev/null; then
    p=$(pgrep -x LaughCounter); echo "RUNNING pid=$p started: $(ps -o lstart= -p "$p")"
  else echo "NOT RUNNING"; fi

  echo; echo "=== crash reports ==="
  find ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports -maxdepth 2 -iname "*laugh*" -print 2>/dev/null | tail -20 || true
  for f in $(find ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports -maxdepth 2 -iname "*laugh*" 2>/dev/null | tail -2); do
    echo "--- $f ---"; sed -n '1,80p' "$f"
  done

  echo; echo "=== real sleep/wake history ==="
  pmset -g log | grep -E "Entering Sleep|Wake from|DarkWake|Sleep Failure|Wake Failure|Hibernate" | tail -120

  echo; echo "=== system log: the LaughCounter process ==="
  log show --last 24h --predicate 'process == "LaughCounter"' --style compact 2>&1 | tail -120

  echo; echo "=== system log: crashes/exceptions naming LaughCounter ==="
  log show --last 24h --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "LaughCounter"' --style compact 2>&1 \
    | grep -iE "crash|exception|terminat|signal|fault|exit" | tail -60

  echo; echo "=== BRIO / USB audio comings and goings ==="
  log show --last 24h --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "BRIO" OR eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "AppleUSBAudio"' \
    --style compact 2>&1 | tail -120

  echo; echo "=== LaughCounter lifecycle lines only ==="
  grep -E "app launched|listening started|listening stopped|could not start|configuration changed|system woke|app terminated" "$LOG" | tail -80
} > "$OUT" 2>&1
echo "wrote $OUT"
```

Takes a couple of minutes (`log show` over 24h is the slow part). What each section decides:

- **running / crash reports** — crash vs. wedged latch. Different fixes; everything else follows from this.
- **real sleep/wake history** — how often it actually sleeps, how long for, and whether wakes are full or dark. Sets the standby threshold I guessed at 5 min.
- **BRIO / USB audio** — how long the mic is gone after each wake and after each teardown. Sets the settle delay I guessed at 2.5s. Yesterday's 7-minute absence, if typical, means my 62-second retry ladder is far too short.
- **lifecycle lines** — whether any wake ever produced a clean `system woke` → `listening started`.

> ⚠️ Heads-up on the PR: whatever this turns out to be, **#59 does not fix it.** Its resume path only runs if the app is alive, and it hangs off sleep/wake — while your actual failures are triggered by audio-device teardowns, twice right after the *display* slept. Don't merge it as the fix. I'd rather rescope it once I see the second file than guess again. No more code until then, as agreed.

     func start(format: AVAudioFormat) throws {
         let input = engine.inputNode
+        // Re-validate the live hardware format right before installing the tap.
+        // The device can vanish or change between prepareFormat() and here (dock
+        // unplug, wake-time re-enumeration), and installTap with a format that no
+        // longer matches the hardware raises an *uncatchable* NSException instead
+        // of throwing. Checking now converts the realistic stale-format cases into
+        // a catchable error the caller's teardown path handles — it narrows the
+        // race window to microseconds but cannot close it entirely (AVAudioEngine
+        // offers nothing atomic), so this path is hardened, not crash-proof.
+        let live = input.outputFormat(forBus: 0)
+        guard live.sampleRate == format.sampleRate,
+              live.channelCount == format.channelCount else {
+            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 2, userInfo: [
+                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
+                    "input device changed between prepare and start "
+                    + "(expected \(format.sampleRate)Hz/\(format.channelCount)ch, "
+                    + "live \(live.sampleRate)Hz/\(live.channelCount)ch)",
+            ])
+        }
         input.removeTap(onBus: 0)   // no-op if none installed; keeps restart clean
         input.installTap(onBus: 0, bufferSize: 8192, format: format) { [weak self] buffer, when in
             self?.onBuffer?(buffer, when)
         }

input.title: macOS app crashes on every audio configuration change (installTap format assertion)
input.body:
Diagnosed from the owner's Mac mini. **Every `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` kills the app** — 6 out of 6 occurrences over 15 days, no survivors. This is the real cause of "the counter isn't running any more"; it is not a sleep/standby problem.

## Evidence

Two crash reports, byte-identical signature, timestamped to the second against the activity log:

```
EXC_CRASH (SIGABRT) — abort() called
required condition is false: format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate

+[NSException raise:format:]
AVAudioEngineImpl::InstallTapOnNode(...)
-[AVAudioNode installTapOnBus:bufferSize:format:block:]
AudioHub.start(format:)
AppDelegate.finishListening()
closure #1 in AppDelegate.requestListening()
```

Every `audio configuration changed — reconfiguring` line in `laughcounter.log` is the **last** line before a hand relaunch — no `listening started`, no `could not start listening`, because an uncaught NSException leaves no chance to log:

| local time | what happened |
|---|---|
| Jul 12 22:11, Jul 13 01:41, Jul 13 11:04, Jul 14 00:52 | config change → dead until relaunched |
| Jul 28 17:38:33 | display sleeps (powerd drops "prevent sleep while display is on") |
| Jul 28 17:38:52 | coreaudiod tears down ~25 audio contexts → config change → **crash** (report `LaughCounter-2026-07-28-173855.ips`) |
| Jul 28 19:35:38 | relaunched by hand |
| Jul 28 19:36:10 | coreaudiod tears down the Logitech BRIO engine → config change → **crash** (`LaughCounter-2026-07-28-193612.ips`), 32s after launch |
| Jul 28 19:43 | BRIO reappears on USB (~7 min absent) |

The longest outage was **15 days** (Jul 13 → Jul 28) with nobody noticing the app was gone.

Machine: Mac mini (Mac16,10), macOS 26.5.2, `sleep 0` / `standby 0` (idle system sleep disabled), `displaysleep 20`. Input is a **Logitech BRIO** USB webcam mic that drops off and re-enumerates. The trigger is a CoreAudio device teardown — twice right after the *display* slept — not a system wake.

## Why the existing guard doesn't stop it

`AudioHub.start(format:)` re-validates before the tap (added in #22):

```swift
let live = input.outputFormat(forBus: 0)
guard live.sampleRate == format.sampleRate, live.channelCount == format.channelCount else { throw … }
```

That reads the **node's output format**, while AVFoundation asserts on the engine's **`inputHWFormat`**. With a single long-lived `AVAudioEngine` (`AudioHub` holds one for the whole process), the node's cached format can still report the old rate — so the guard compares stale against stale, passes, and `installTap` then fails against the freshly-queried hardware format. The 6/6 hit rate says this is deterministic, not the microsecond race the code comments assume.

**Caveat:** the crashing binary is **pre-#22** — the backtrace shows `finishListening()` with no arguments, and `finishListening(generation:)` only exists after `beda6cb`. The owner's `/Applications/LaughCounter.app` was installed around Jul 12; the `v0.2.1` Release asset has since been rebuilt from `main`. So step one is to reinstall the current DMG and see whether the #22 guard downgrades the crash to the catchable `input device changed between prepare and start` error. The reasoning above says it probably won't, but that has to be measured, not assumed.

## Proposed fix, if it still crashes

1. **`installTap(onBus:bufferSize:format: nil)`** — passing nil uses the node's own format, so `format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate` cannot fail. The analyzer then has to be configured from the first delivered buffer's `format` rather than pre-configured.
2. **Build a fresh `AVAudioEngine` per restart** instead of holding one for the process lifetime, so no stale cached hardware format survives a device change.
3. **An Objective-C `@try/@catch` shim** around the tap install as a backstop — Swift cannot catch NSException, and AVFAudio raises several. A small ObjC target in `Package.swift` is enough.
4. Consider a launchd `KeepAlive` agent so an always-on box recovers even from a crash we didn't anticipate.

Also worth noting: a crash means `applicationWillTerminate` never runs, so each of these 6 crashes skipped the release-the-mic teardown that #22 exists to guarantee. That doc calls crash-path teardown "residual risk, not a bug" — at 6 crashes in 15 days it is no longer residual.

## Relationship to #60 / PR #59

PR #59 (return-from-standby resume) does not address this and must not be merged as the fix — its resume path only runs if the process is alive, and it hangs off sleep/wake notifications while these failures are triggered by audio-device teardowns. It stays useful on its own terms; this issue is the one that explains the symptom.

```bash

echo "--- app bundle date ---"; ls -ld /Applications/LaughCounter.app
echo "--- app frames in the new crash ---"

The discriminator is one symbol:

- **`AppDelegate.finishListening(generation:)`** → you're on the current build. #22's guard is confirmed insufficient, exactly as I predicted, and there's nothing left to test — I go straight to the fix.

For what it's worth I expect the first branch. The guard reads the node's cached format while AVFoundation asserts on the live hardware format, and a process-lifetime `AVAudioEngine` keeps that cache stale — that's a design gap the guard can't close, not a race it can narrow.

That last detail is the important one — the crash is what wedged your webcam.

When the app dies on an uncaught exception, `applicationWillTerminate` never runs, so the input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is never torn down. That's precisely the failure mode #22 was built to prevent, and its doc calls the crash path "uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug." Three crashes in nine hours, one wedged BRIO needing a physical re-plug: it's not residual any more. Fixing the crash fixes the wedge.

**On which binary crashed:** `/Applications/LaughCounter.app` is dated **Jul 28 20:09** — the original install was Jul 12, so that's your reinstall of the current build. And there's no `could not start listening: input device changed…` line, meaning #22's guard *passed* and `installTap` asserted anyway. That's the outcome I predicted: the guard reads the node's cached format while AVFoundation asserts on the live hardware format, and a process-lifetime `AVAudioEngine` keeps that cache stale. So the guard can't close this — it's a design gap, not a race.

(The symbol check didn't run — macOS has no `python3` without dev tools, my mistake. If you want the belt-and-braces confirmation, this needs nothing extra: `grep -o 'finishListening[^"]*' ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/LaughCounter-2026-07-29-012940.ips | sort -u | head -3` — `finishListening(generation:)` confirms the new build. I'm confident enough from the bundle date to proceed without it.)

**Right now, while it's late:** quit LaughCounter from its menu (⌘Q) rather than leaving it running. A clean quit releases the mic properly; every crash risks wedging the BRIO again. You'll lose counting until the fix ships, but you won't lose the webcam.

The fix for #61, concretely:
1. **A fresh `AVAudioEngine` per start** instead of one for the process lifetime — the structural fix, so no stale cached hardware format can survive a device change. `AudioHub` takes ownership of the config-change observer, since re-creating the engine invalidates an observer registered against the old instance.
2. **`installTap(format: nil)`** — the node's own format, so `format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate` cannot fail by construction. The analyzer then configures from the first buffer's `format`, which needs a small reorder in `LaughDetector`.

1	# LaughCounter for macOS (native menu-bar app)
2	
3	The clean way to run LaughCounter on a Mac: a tiny menu-bar app that uses only
4	**built-in macOS frameworks** — nothing to install, nothing left behind.
5	
6	- **Detects laughter** with Apple's built-in Sound Analysis (no model download).
7	- **Counts** distinct laughs and **logs** them to
8	  `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl` (no audio saved).
9	- **😄 menu-bar icon** shows today's count — that's your "it's running" light.
10	- **A soft blip** plays when a laugh is logged.
11	- **Say “I just laughed”** and it logs a laugh it missed, blipping **twice** to
12	  confirm (on-device speech recognition — nothing leaves your Mac). There's also a
13	  menu item / ⌘L if you'd rather click.
14	
15	## Get it (no Xcode needed)
16	
17	**⬇️ [Download the latest LaughCounter.dmg](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)** — this link always points at the most recent published release.
18	
19	Prefer a specific build, or no release published yet? The app is also built for
20	every change by GitHub Actions on a macOS runner:
21	
22	1. Go to the repo's **Actions** tab → open the latest **“Build macOS DMG”** run.
23	2. Download the **`LaughCounter-dmg`** artifact and unzip it to get `LaughCounter.dmg`.
24	
25	*(Releases are published by pushing a `v*` tag — see “Cutting a release” below.)*
26	
27	## Install
28	
29	1. Open `LaughCounter.dmg` and drag **LaughCounter** into **Applications**.
30	2. **Get past Gatekeeper (first launch only).** The app is ad-hoc signed but not
31	   notarized (that needs a paid Apple Developer account), so macOS blocks the first
32	   open with *“Apple could not verify LaughCounter is free of malware.”* Clear it
33	   **one of two ways**:
34	   - **System Settings:** click **Done** on the warning, then open **System
35	     Settings → Privacy & Security**, scroll to **Security**, and click **Open
36	     Anyway** next to *“LaughCounter was blocked…”*. Confirm **Open Anyway** again.
37	   - **Terminal (most reliable):** after dragging it to Applications, run
38	     `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/LaughCounter.app`, then open it
39	     normally.
40	
41	   > On **macOS 15 (Sequoia)** the old **right-click → Open** shortcut no longer
42	   > bypasses this — you must use one of the two methods above.
43	3. Approve **Microphone** and **Speech Recognition** when prompted.
44	4. A 😄 with a number appears in your menu bar. That's it.
45	
46	**Always-on:** add it to **System Settings → General → Login Items** so it starts
47	with the Mac. **Uninstall:** quit it, drag the app to the Trash, and (optionally)
48	delete `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/`.
49	
50	## Build it yourself (optional, on a Mac)
51	
52	```bash
53	cd mac
54	bash scripts/build-app.sh     # -> dist/LaughCounter.app  (bakes AppIcon.icns)
55	bash scripts/make-dmg.sh      # -> dist/LaughCounter.dmg  (with the 😄 volume icon)
56	```
57	
58	Requires the Swift toolchain (Xcode Command Line Tools). No third-party packages,
59	and no toolchain beyond what macOS ships. The committed `Resources/AppIcon.png`
60	master is turned into a multi-resolution `.icns` at build time with
61	`sips`/`iconutil` — replace that PNG to change the icon.
62	
63	This produces an **ad-hoc-signed** app (the Gatekeeper step under *Install*
64	applies). To instead sign it with a real **Developer ID** and notarize it — so it
65	opens with no warning — you need a paid Apple Developer account, then:
66	
67	```bash
68	export MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)"
69	bash scripts/build-app.sh          # signs with Hardened Runtime + entitlements
70	bash scripts/make-dmg.sh
71	export APPLE_ID=you@example.com APPLE_TEAM_ID=XXXXXXXXXX APPLE_APP_PASSWORD=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx
72	bash scripts/notarize-dmg.sh       # submits to Apple + staples the ticket
73	```
74	
75	Both DMG workflows do this automatically when the matching repository secrets are
76	set (`MACOS_CERT_P12`, `MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD`, `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`,
77	`APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `APPLE_APP_PASSWORD`) — so published releases open with no
78	warning. This is the **non–App Store** path; a Mac App Store build additionally
79	requires the App Sandbox and a different (Apple Distribution) certificate.
80	
81	## Cutting a release
82	
83	Releases publish **automatically**. On every push to `main` that touches `mac/**`,
84	the **Release macOS DMG** workflow builds the app, packages the DMG, and
85	creates/updates the GitHub Release for the app's current version (read from
86	`Info.plist`), attaching `LaughCounter.dmg` — which is what the
87	[latest-release download link](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)
88	resolves to.
89	
90	So to **ship a new version**, bump `CFBundleShortVersionString` in
91	`Resources/Info.plist` and merge to `main` — a new `v<version>` Release appears on
92	its own. (Merges that keep the same version just refresh that Release's DMG.) You
93	can also publish a Release from the GitHub UI, or run the workflow manually from
94	the Actions tab.
95	
96	## The laugh log
97	
98	Laughs are appended to `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl`,
99	one JSON object per line, fields in a fixed order:
100	
101	| field | meaning |
102	|-------|---------|
103	| `start_iso` | human-readable start time (ISO-8601) |
104	| `label` | `auto` (detected), `missed` (you told us we missed one), `candidate` (sub-threshold — logged for tuning, **not counted**), `rejected` (not counted) |
105	| `start` / `end` | epoch seconds of the laugh's real start/end (from the classifier's window timing) |
106	| `peak` | highest laughter confidence during the laugh (0–1, rounded) |
107	| `duration` | `end − start` in seconds. **Coarse:** the built-in classifier analyses in ~3s windows, so a single laugh reads ~3s; only laughs spanning several windows read longer. It's a rough length, not a precise one. |
108	| `mean` | average laughter confidence across the laugh |
109	| `source` | `mic` (auto), `voice` (spoken “I just laughed”), `button` (menu / ⌘L) |
110	| `origin` | you-vs-TV **hypothesis**: `me` or `tv` |
111	| `tv_signal` | strongest produced-audio context (0–1) the hypothesis is based on |
112	| `origin_reason` | plain-language why (e.g. `music=0.66 (soundtrack/audience) → TV`) |
113	| `type` | which laugh class fired (e.g. giggle, chuckle), when known |
114	| `context` | top competing non-laugh classes heard |
115	
116	**You vs the TV (two counters).** The menu bar shows `😄 N  📺 M` — your laughs vs
117	the TV's, today. Each laugh gets a *hypothesis*, not a verdict: a strong
118	produced-audio context (music, dialogue, audience, instruments — `tv_signal ≥ 0.3`)
119	is attributed to the TV; clean laughter with little of that is attributed to you.
120	Only *your* laughs blip. It will guess wrong sometimes (a real laugh over TV music),
121	which is why every laugh is still logged with its reasoning — nothing is discarded.
122	The class-based classifier can't hear *who* laughed; a loudness/proximity signal and,

# CI & release — the macOS DMG

How `LaughCounter.dmg` reaches users, and the workflow-trigger gotchas learned
wiring it up. Read before editing `.github/workflows/release-macos-dmg.yml` or
`build-macos-dmg.yml`.

**The shape.** `release-macos-dmg.yml` owns `main`: on a push to `main` touching
`mac/**` it builds the DMG, derives `v<version>` from `mac/Resources/Info.plist`,
and creates/updates that GitHub Release with `LaughCounter.dmg` attached — so the
README's stable `releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg` link always resolves.
`build-macos-dmg.yml` is the feature-branch artifact builder and **excludes
`main`** (`branches: ["**", "!main"]`) so it never duplicates the release build.

## Trigger the release on push-to-main, not a `v*` tag push

A Claude Code **web session pushes through a git-only proxy that cannot push
`v*` tags**, so a release workflow keyed on `push: tags` never fires from a
session — the Release area stays empty and the `latest/download` link 404s. Key
the release on **push to `main`** (scoped to `mac/**`) instead: the job derives
`v<version>` from `Info.plist` and creates the tag + Release with `GITHUB_TOKEN`,
which *can* tag and release from within Actions even though the session can't.
(#18 / #19)

## A UI-published Release does not fire `push: tags` — add `release: published`

Publishing a Release from the GitHub UI creates the tag but does **not** emit a
`push: tags` event, so a workflow listening only for tag pushes won't build for
it. Keep a `release: types: [published]` trigger alongside the push-to-main one so
a hand-published Release still builds and attaches the DMG. (#11 / #13)

## Why the two triggers don't loop or double-build

- The tag + Release the push-to-main job creates is made with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and
  a Release created by `GITHUB_TOKEN` does **not** re-fire the `release` event —
  so the `release: published` trigger doesn't re-run it. (This is the canon's
  general "`GITHUB_TOKEN` doesn't start another workflow" rule, applied to the
  `release` event specifically.)
- `build-macos-dmg.yml` excludes `main`, so a `mac/**` push to `main` builds once
  (in the release job), not twice.

## Signing & notarization is an optional, secret-gated lane (#4)

Both DMG workflows have an **optional** Developer ID signing + Apple notarization
lane that runs only when the signing secrets are set (`MACOS_CERT_P12`,
`MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD`, `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`,
`APPLE_APP_PASSWORD`); without them the build still passes and ships an **ad-hoc**
DMG. **Keep it secret-gated** — never make signing a required step, or a fork or
secret-less build breaks. The signing/notarization how-to and the user-facing
Gatekeeper steps live in `mac/README.md`; `scripts/build-app.sh` signs and
`scripts/notarize-dmg.sh` notarizes + staples. The CI-side gotchas that aren't in
the README:

- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`),
  and under it the mic needs an explicit entitlement
  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, in
  `mac/Resources/LaughCounter.entitlements`) that an ad-hoc build doesn't — so
  turning on notarization silently kills mic access unless the entitlement ships
  with it. (Speech recognition is gated by TCC + the Info.plist usage string, not
  a codesign entitlement, so it needs nothing there.)
- **An ad-hoc signature can't be notarized** — they're separate lanes; only the
  Developer-ID-signed `.app` (built when `MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY` is set) can be
  submitted to the notary service.
- **The ephemeral signing keychain must be added to the searchable keychain
  list** (`security list-keychains -d user -s "$KEYCHAIN" $(security
  list-keychains -d user | sed …)`) or `codesign` can't find the imported
  identity. That `sed` pipe is why the workflows set `defaults.run.shell: bash`
  for pipefail (#27; enforced by the canon `gha/run-pipefail` check).
- **macOS 15 (Sequoia) removed the right-click → Open Gatekeeper bypass** — the
  ad-hoc install path is now System Settings → Privacy & Security → *Open Anyway*,
  or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>` (see `mac/README.md`).
- This is the **non–App Store** track (no App Sandbox); a Mac App Store build
  would need the App Sandbox and a different Apple Distribution certificate.

## Never reuse an `AVAudioEngine` across a device change (#61)

An `AVAudioEngine` caches the input hardware format when its input node is first
materialized, and **the cache does not follow the device**. After CoreAudio tears
the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod dropping its contexts
when the display sleeps — `inputNode.outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports the
*old* rate, while `installTap` validates against the freshly-queried hardware
format. They disagree, and `installTap` raises an **uncatchable** NSException:
`required condition is false: format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate`.

This killed the app on **every** configuration change — six for six over fifteen
days on the owner's Mac mini, the longest outage fifteen days of nobody noticing.
The pre-tap guard added in #22 did not help, because it compared the stale cache
against itself and always passed: not the microsecond race its comment assumed,
but a design gap. So `AudioHub.prepareFormat()` **builds a new engine every time**
(stopping the old one first — dropping the last reference to a *running* engine
abandons its IOProc on the device, the wedge condition). Three consequences:

- **The crash was also the mic-wedge cause.** An uncaught NSException aborts the
  process, so `applicationWillTerminate` never runs and the tap's IOProc is left
  registered — the BRIO went dead until physically re-plugged. The exit-path rule
  below calls crash teardown "residual risk"; at six crashes in fifteen days it
  was the main risk.
- **A replaced engine invalidates an observer bound to the old instance**, so
  `AudioHub` owns the `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` observation and
  republishes it via `onConfigurationChange` (delivered on main). Registering it
  from `AppDelegate` against `audio.engine` would go quiet after the first
  restart — and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
  its microphone vanished.
- **Swift cannot catch `NSException`**, so the last line of defence is a few
  lines of Objective-C (`Sources/ObjCExceptionTrap`, its own SwiftPM target — our
  source, not a dependency). Catching one is only safe because `installTap`
  validates *before* mutating anything; don't wrap framework calls in general.

Reproduce it without waiting for hardware to misbehave: let the display sleep
(`displaysleep 20`), and coreaudiod tears its contexts down seconds later.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# macOS audio lifecycle — releasing the mic on every path

Hard-won rules for `mac/Sources/LaughCounter/` (AudioHub, AppDelegate's restart
machinery, VoiceCommand). Read before touching engine start/stop, sleep/wake, or
exit handling.

**The invariant.** If this process ends — or intentionally stops capture — while
the `AVAudioEngine` input tap's CoreAudio IOProc is still registered on the
device, some USB webcam mics wedge: dead/silent, no input registered in System
Settings, until physically re-plugged. So the tap + engine must be torn down on
*every* path where capture ends, and the engine must never rapid-cycle or
overlap restarts. (#22)

## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit path" by itself

`NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
`applicationWillTerminate` — but **NSApplication installs no signal handlers**:
a bare SIGTERM (Activity Monitor "Quit", `killall`), SIGINT (Ctrl-C in a dev
terminal), or SIGHUP kills the process with no teardown. `main.swift` routes
those through `DispatchSourceSignal` → `NSApp.terminate`; the `signal(sig,
SIG_IGN)` must precede `resume()` or a signal in the gap still takes the fatal
default. SIGKILL/Force-Quit/crash remain uncoverable — residual risk, not a bug.
Don't add `NSSupportsSuddenTermination` to Info.plist: it would let logout
SIGKILL the app past all of this.

## Deferred work must be generation-guarded

`asyncAfter` timers scheduled before sleep **fire immediately on wake** — so any
delayed engine start (the +0.4s `finishListening`, the +1.0s wake resume) that a
stop raced with would otherwise re-acquire the mic going *into* sleep or
un-settled at wake. Every intentional stop bumps `restartGeneration`; every
delayed closure captures the generation at schedule time and aborts if it moved.
When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /
`restartQueued` / `suppressConfigChange`, or the latches stay stuck and block
all future starts.

## There is no "returned from standby" notification — fan in, then coalesce

macOS distinguishes sleep depths internally but exposes no standby-specific event:
`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires
several of them in a burst and each must not schedule its own restart:

- **Coalesce with an id, not a bool.** `pendingResumeID` holds the one in-flight
  resume; a stale timer compares its captured id and returns without touching
  state. A bare `resumePending` bool deadlocks: a re-sleep during the delay
  invalidates the timer, the timer clears the bool, and whichever of the two
  orderings loses leaves the next wake either unable to schedule (flag stuck true)
  or double-scheduling.
- **Gate on owing a resume**, i.e. `sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening)`.
  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
  three workspace triggers still cover the case.

## Resume by *intent*, and retry — a failed post-standby start has no second event

`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.

The intent is stored as `offReason: String?` — nil means "meant to be running" and
`listeningIntent` is derived from it — rather than a bool beside a separate reason
string. The menu status, the tooltip and the wake log all render that one field, so
they cannot disagree about whether the counter is off or why ("paused",
"no microphone access", "starting up"). Menu **Pause listening** sets it; every
request to listen clears it, which is what asking to listen means.

After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and the mic can still be
re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every
success / system return / manual resume. Bounded on purpose (a mic that is gone for
good emits nothing and must not be polled forever) and slow on purpose (rapid-cycling
is what wedges the mic). The wake settle is also stretched 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep
lasted longer than `standbyThreshold`; measure that span with `Date()`, **not**
`ProcessInfo.systemUptime`, which does not advance while the machine is asleep.

## Config-change suppression must reconcile, not just drop

CoreAudio posts `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` for our *own* stop/start
(react → infinite restart loop, hence the suppress window) **and** for genuine
device events — including while the machine heads into sleep (hence the
`sleeping` gate from `willSleep` until the post-wake settle). A genuine event
swallowed by the window is reconciled at settle time by *state*, not by the
notification: engine dead while `listening` → restart; start failed and an
event arrived → one retry per swallowed event (a dead mic emits no events, so
this can't poll).

## Misc gotchas that bit

- `engine.stop()` unconditionally in `AudioHub.stop()`: it's safe when not
  running and it releases what `prepare()` allocated — a prepare-then-throw
  path would otherwise keep the input unit holding the device.
- `installTap` with a format the hardware no longer matches raises an
  **uncatchable NSException** — re-validate the live format immediately before
  the tap (narrows, doesn't eliminate; there is no atomic API).
- `SFSpeechRecognizer` fed via `SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest` never
  holds the device — it can't cause the wedge. But its state is touched from
  main, the Speech callback queue, *and* the audio tap thread: everything in
  `VoiceCommand` goes through one lock, and the two-phase `start()` gates the
  task store on *request identity* (`request === newRequest`), because a
  restart() between the phases leaves `running == true` — gating on `running`
  would store a dead task and permanently block the idempotency guard.

+- **A replaced engine invalidates an observer bound to the old instance**, so
+  `AudioHub` owns the `.AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange` observation and
+  republishes it via `onConfigurationChange` (delivered on main). Registering it
+  from `AppDelegate` against `audio.engine` would go quiet after the first
+  restart — and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
+  its microphone vanished.
+- **Swift cannot catch `NSException`**, so the last line of defence is a few
+  lines of Objective-C (`Sources/ObjCExceptionTrap`, its own SwiftPM target — our
+  source, not a dependency). Catching one is only safe because `installTap`
+  validates *before* mutating anything; don't wrap framework calls in general.
+
+Reproduce it without waiting for hardware to misbehave: let the display sleep
+(`displaysleep 20`), and coreaudiod tears its contexts down seconds later.
+

 `NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the logout/shutdown quit Apple Event) runs
@@ -34,6 +71,57 @@ When cancelling in-flight restarts, also reset `restartInFlight` /

 all future starts.
 
+## There is no "returned from standby" notification — fan in, then coalesce
+
+macOS distinguishes sleep depths internally but exposes no standby-specific event:
+`NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` is all you get, and it is **not equivalent to "the
+machine is back"** — a dark/Power-Nap wake fires it with nobody there and the Mac
+re-sleeps moments later. So `systemDidReturn(reason:)` fans in four signals —
+`didWake`, `screensDidWake`, `sessionDidBecomeActive`, and the distributed
+`com.apple.screenIsUnlocked` — and coalesces them, because a real return fires
+several of them in a burst and each must not schedule its own restart:
+
+- **Coalesce with an id, not a bool.** `pendingResumeID` holds the one in-flight
+  resume; a stale timer compares its captured id and returns without touching
+  state. A bare `resumePending` bool deadlocks: a re-sleep during the delay
+  invalidates the timer, the timer clears the bool, and whichever of the two
+  orderings loses leaves the next wake either unable to schedule (flag stuck true)
+  or double-scheduling.

+  Displays wake and sessions activate with no sleep involved (screensaver, user
+  switching); reacting to those would cycle a healthy engine — the wedge condition.
+- **Always ungate `sleeping` in the resume timer**, even on the "stay off" path, or
+  `requestListening` stays blocked forever and the menu's Start item does nothing.
+- The distributed unlock notification is free here because the app is
+  non–App Store (no App Sandbox). Under the sandbox it silently never arrives; the
+  three workspace triggers still cover the case.
+

+
+`listening` ("the engine is running") is not the state a wake should branch on.
+`listeningIntent` ("the counter is meant to be running") is: sleep suspends capture
+without clearing it, so a return reactivates only a counter that was actually
+active, while a start that merely *failed* keeps it and stays eligible for recovery.
+Branching on `listening` instead would make any pre-sleep failure permanent.
+
+The intent is stored as `offReason: String?` — nil means "meant to be running" and
+`listeningIntent` is derived from it — rather than a bool beside a separate reason
+string. The menu status, the tooltip and the wake log all render that one field, so
+they cannot disagree about whether the counter is off or why ("paused",
+"no microphone access", "starting up"). Menu **Pause listening** sets it; every
+request to listen clears it, which is what asking to listen means.
+

+re-enumerating when the settle window closes. That start throws, and — unlike the
+config-change cases — **nothing else will ever fire** to recover from it, so the app
+sits silently "not listening" until someone opens the menu. Hence
+`scheduleStartRetry`: doubling 2s → 32s, capped at `maxStartRetries`, reset on every
+success / system return / manual resume. Bounded on purpose (a mic that is gone for
+good emits nothing and must not be polled forever) and slow on purpose (rapid-cycling
+is what wedges the mic). The wake settle is also stretched 1.0s → 2.5s when the sleep
+lasted longer than `standbyThreshold`; measure that span with `Date()`, **not**
+`ProcessInfo.systemUptime`, which does not advance while the machine is asleep.
+

first materialized, and that cache does not follow the device. After
CoreAudio tears the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod
dropping its contexts when the display sleeps — outputFormat(forBus:0) keeps
reporting the old rate while installTap validates against the live hardware
format. The pre-tap guard from #22 could never catch it: it compared the
stale cache against itself and always passed. Not the microsecond race its
comment assumed — a design gap.

So prepareFormat() now builds a fresh engine every time, stopping the old one
first (dropping the last reference to a running engine would abandon its
IOProc on the device, which is the wedge condition #22 exists to prevent).

Because the engine instance now changes, AudioHub owns the configuration-change
observation and republishes it through onConfigurationChange; an observer
registered by AppDelegate against audio.engine would have gone quiet after the
first restart, and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing
that its microphone vanished.

few lines of Objective-C in their own SwiftPM target (our source, not a
dependency) turn anything still raised by installTap into an ordinary error
the existing teardown and retry path handles.

This crash was also the mic-wedge cause: an uncaught exception aborts the
process, so applicationWillTerminate never ran and the tap's IOProc stayed
registered — the webcam mic went dead until physically re-plugged.

rebuild the audio engine per start — installTap crashed on every device change

The app died on every .AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange: six for six over
fifteen days on the owner's Mac mini, three crash reports with an identical
signature, the longest outage fifteen days of nobody noticing the counter
was gone.

    required condition is false: format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate
    -[AVAudioNode installTapOnBus:bufferSize:format:block:]
    AudioHub.start(format:) / AppDelegate.finishListening()

An AVAudioEngine caches the input hardware format when its input node is
first materialized, and that cache does not follow the device. After
CoreAudio tears the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod
dropping its contexts when the display sleeps — outputFormat(forBus:0) keeps
reporting the old rate while installTap validates against the live hardware
format. The pre-tap guard from #22 could never catch it: it compared the
stale cache against itself and always passed. Not the microsecond race its
comment assumed — a design gap.

So prepareFormat() now builds a fresh engine every time, stopping the old one
first (dropping the last reference to a running engine would abandon its
IOProc on the device, which is the wedge condition #22 exists to prevent).

Because the engine instance now changes, AudioHub owns the configuration-change
observation and republishes it through onConfigurationChange; an observer
registered by AppDelegate against audio.engine would have gone quiet after the
first restart, and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing
that its microphone vanished.

Adds ObjCExceptionTrap as a backstop — Swift cannot catch NSException, so a
few lines of Objective-C in their own SwiftPM target (our source, not a
dependency) turn anything still raised by installTap into an ordinary error
the existing teardown and retry path handles.

This crash was also the mic-wedge cause: an uncaught exception aborts the
process, so applicationWillTerminate never ran and the tap's IOProc stayed
registered — the webcam mic went dead until physically re-plugged.

Closes #61

@@ -0,0 +1,36 @@
+#import <Foundation/Foundation.h>
+
+NS_ASSUME_NONNULL_BEGIN
+
+/// Runs a block, converting an Objective-C `NSException` into an `NSError`.
+///
+/// Swift has no way to catch `NSException` — `do/catch` only sees Swift errors,
+/// so an exception raised inside a Cocoa framework call unwinds straight past
+/// Swift code and aborts the process. AVFoundation raises them as *precondition*
+/// checks: `-[AVAudioNode installTapOnBus:bufferSize:format:block:]` raises
+/// `com.apple.coreaudio.avfaudio` ("required condition is false:
+/// format.sampleRate == inputHWFormat.sampleRate") when the tap format no longer
+/// matches the live input hardware, which killed this app on every audio device
+/// change (#61). A few lines of Objective-C are the only way to survive one.
+///
+/// Catching an exception from an arbitrary framework is not generally safe — the
+/// framework may be left half-mutated. It is safe for the call wrapped here
+/// because it raises *before* doing any work: the condition is validated at the
+/// top of the call, so nothing has changed when the exception is thrown. Wrap
+/// only calls known to behave that way, not framework calls in general.
+@interface ObjCExceptionTrap : NSObject
+
+/// Runs `block`. Returns `YES` if it completed, or `NO` having set `error` to a
+/// description of the `NSException` it raised. Imported into Swift as a throwing
+/// call, so callers write `try ObjCExceptionTrap.run { … }`.
+///
+/// The selector is `run:` so it survives Swift's import unchanged. `perform:`
+/// would collide with `NSObject`'s own `perform(_:)`, and `runBlock:` imports as
+/// `run(_:)` anyway — Swift strips a trailing noun that just restates the
+/// argument type, and then marks the spelled-out name obsolete.
++ (BOOL)run:(void (NS_NOESCAPE ^)(void))block
+      error:(NSError *_Nullable *_Nullable)error;
+
+@end
+
+NS_ASSUME_NONNULL_END
